questions.q:
A 37-year-old woman with low back pain for the past 4 weeks wants to know if you recommend surgery. You prefer to base your treatment recommendations on research evidence whenever possible. In the strongest study you can find, investigators reviewed the medical records of 40 consecutive men with low back pain under care at their clinic—22 had been referred for surgery and the other 18 patients had remained under medical care without surgery. The study compared rates of disabling pain after 2 months. All of the surgically treated patients and 10 of the medically treated patients were still being seen in the clinic throughout this time. Rates of pain relief were slightly higher in the surgically treated patients.

Because there are relatively few patients in this study, it may give a misleading impression of the actual effectiveness of surgery.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias is a systematic problem in how the compared groups were assembled, so they differ in more than the treatment. A small number of patients does not make the groups systematically different; it makes the result vulnerable to random variation, which is chance.
Measurement bias

Measurement bias is a systematic error from the way an outcome or exposure is measured, such as unstandardized methods or unequal detection between groups. The number of patients says nothing about how pain was measured; too few patients is a problem of random variation instead.
Confounding

Confounding needs a covariate that is associated with both the treatment and the outcome so its effect cannot be separated from the treatment effect. A statement about having few patients names no such covariate; the concern is random variation, which is chance.
Chance

Correct. Chance is random variation producing conclusions that differ from the true results, and a small sample can give a misleading impression of the population it came from. Statistical analysis can estimate chance, and good design reduces it, but it is never totally eliminated.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity is the degree to which results also hold true in other patients and clinical settings. The worry here is different: with so few patients, random variation may make even the observed difference misleading, and that is chance rather than generalizability.

questions.q:
A 37-year-old woman with low back pain for the past 4 weeks wants to know if you recommend surgery. You prefer to base your treatment recommendations on research evidence whenever possible. In the strongest study you can find, investigators reviewed the medical records of 40 consecutive men with low back pain under care at their clinic—22 had been referred for surgery and the other 18 patients had remained under medical care without surgery. The study compared rates of disabling pain after 2 months. All of the surgically treated patients and 10 of the medically treated patients were still being seen in the clinic throughout this time. Rates of pain relief were slightly higher in the surgically treated patients.

The results of this study may not apply to your patient, a woman, because all the patients in the study were men.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias concerns how the compared groups inside a study were assembled so that they differ in more than the treatment. Both treatment groups were all men, so sex does not make them differ; the limitation is who the findings apply to.
Measurement bias

Measurement bias is incorrect results caused by the method of measurement. Nothing about how pain was measured is described; the point is that a study done only in men may not apply to a woman, which is a question of generalizability.
Confounding

Confounding needs a covariate that differs between the treatment groups and is tied to both treatment and outcome. Every patient was a man in both groups, so sex cannot differ between them and cannot confound; it only limits applying the results to a woman.
Chance

Chance is random variation that produces results differing from the truth. The concern here is not random error in the men studied but whether these patients, all men, represent this patient, a woman.
External validity (generalizability)

Correct. External validity, also called generalizability, is the degree to which results are also true in other clinical settings and patients. Applying a study of men to a woman assumes surgery works the same way in both sexes, and this is rarely settled by a single study.

questions.q:
A 37-year-old woman with low back pain for the past 4 weeks wants to know if you recommend surgery. You prefer to base your treatment recommendations on research evidence whenever possible. In the strongest study you can find, investigators reviewed the medical records of 40 consecutive men with low back pain under care at their clinic—22 had been referred for surgery and the other 18 patients had remained under medical care without surgery. The study compared rates of disabling pain after 2 months. All of the surgically treated patients and 10 of the medically treated patients were still being seen in the clinic throughout this time. Rates of pain relief were slightly higher in the surgically treated patients.

Fewer patients who did not have surgery remained under care at the clinic 2 months after surgery.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias concerns how the compared groups were assembled, and here the groups were formed by referral for surgery or not. Fewer medically treated patients remaining under care is a different problem: the pain outcome could not be observed equally in the two groups, which makes measurement bias the better fit.
Measurement bias

Correct. Measurement bias means participants in one group are more likely than another to have their outcome detected. All the surgically treated patients but only 10 of 18 medically treated patients stayed under care, so pain was not measured with equal completeness in the two groups.
Confounding

Confounding needs a covariate that is associated with both treatment and outcome. Unequal follow-up is not a patient characteristic that travels with treatment and recovery; it is a difference in how completely the outcome could be observed, which is a measurement problem.
Chance

Chance is random variation, equally likely to push a result higher or lower. Fewer medically treated patients remaining under care is a systematic difference between the groups in outcome detection, so it is bias, not chance.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity asks whether results apply to other patients and settings. Unequal follow-up affects whether the results are correct for the patients who were actually studied, which makes it a threat to internal validity, not generalizability.

questions.q:
A 37-year-old woman with low back pain for the past 4 weeks wants to know if you recommend surgery. You prefer to base your treatment recommendations on research evidence whenever possible. In the strongest study you can find, investigators reviewed the medical records of 40 consecutive men with low back pain under care at their clinic—22 had been referred for surgery and the other 18 patients had remained under medical care without surgery. The study compared rates of disabling pain after 2 months. All of the surgically treated patients and 10 of the medically treated patients were still being seen in the clinic throughout this time. Rates of pain relief were slightly higher in the surgically treated patients.

The patients who were referred for surgery were younger and fitter than those who remained under medical care.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Correct. Selection bias occurs when compared groups differ in more than the focus of the study. Patients referred for surgery were younger and fitter, so better recovery may reflect who was chosen for surgery rather than what surgery did.
Measurement bias

Measurement bias comes from the way an outcome is measured. Age and fitness describe how the patients who were referred differ from those who were not, which is about how the groups were assembled and not about how pain was measured.
Confounding

Age and fitness could act as covariates, but confounding is the inability to separate a covariate's effect from the studied variable during analysis, and it can itself result from selection bias. The statement stresses which patients were referred to surgery, which is how the groups were selected, so selection bias is the better description.
Chance

Chance is random variation, which would not consistently place younger, fitter patients in the surgical group. A consistent difference in the kind of patients in the two groups is systematic, so it is bias rather than chance.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity concerns applying results to other populations. A difference between the two treatment groups inside the study threatens internal validity, the degree to which results are correct for the patients studied, not generalizability.

questions.q:
A 37-year-old woman with low back pain for the past 4 weeks wants to know if you recommend surgery. You prefer to base your treatment recommendations on research evidence whenever possible. In the strongest study you can find, investigators reviewed the medical records of 40 consecutive men with low back pain under care at their clinic—22 had been referred for surgery and the other 18 patients had remained under medical care without surgery. The study compared rates of disabling pain after 2 months. All of the surgically treated patients and 10 of the medically treated patients were still being seen in the clinic throughout this time. Rates of pain relief were slightly higher in the surgically treated patients.

Compared with patients who had medical care alone, patients who had surgery might have been less likely to report whatever pain they had and the treating physicians might have been less inclined to record pain in the medical record.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias concerns how patients ended up in each group. This statement is about how pain was reported and recorded after treatment, which is the measurement of the outcome and not the assembly of the groups.
Measurement bias

Correct. Measurement bias means the method of measuring leads to incorrect results, including when one group is less likely to have its outcome detected. If surgical patients reported less pain and physicians recorded less pain for them, the outcome was measured unequally between the groups.
Confounding

Confounding involves a covariate associated with both treatment and outcome. Differences in how pain is reported and recorded are errors in obtaining the outcome measurement itself, not a patient characteristic linked to both treatment and recovery.
Chance

Chance is random variation, equally likely to push results higher or lower. Systematically less reporting and less recording of pain in one group pushes results in a single direction, which is bias rather than chance.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity is about whether results hold in other patients and settings. Unequal reporting and recording of pain undermines whether the results are correct for the patients studied, which is internal validity.

questions.q:
A 37-year-old woman with low back pain for the past 4 weeks wants to know if you recommend surgery. You prefer to base your treatment recommendations on research evidence whenever possible. In the strongest study you can find, investigators reviewed the medical records of 40 consecutive men with low back pain under care at their clinic—22 had been referred for surgery and the other 18 patients had remained under medical care without surgery. The study compared rates of disabling pain after 2 months. All of the surgically treated patients and 10 of the medically treated patients were still being seen in the clinic throughout this time. Rates of pain relief were slightly higher in the surgically treated patients.

Patients without other medical conditions were both more likely to recover and more likely to be referred for surgery.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias is bias in how the groups were assembled. The statement names a third variable, absence of other medical conditions, that is tied to both receiving surgery and recovering; that pattern defines confounding, even though confounding can sometimes result from selection bias.
Measurement bias

Measurement bias comes from incorrect or unequal measurement of the outcome or exposure. Nothing here concerns how recovery was measured; the problem is that another medical condition is related to both treatment and outcome.
Confounding

Correct. Confounding occurs when a covariate is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, so its effect cannot be separated from the effect of the treatment. Having no other medical conditions makes patients more likely to be referred for surgery and more likely to recover, and it could explain the difference by itself.
Chance

Chance is random variation with no consistent direction. Absence of other conditions is a specific factor that pushes both surgical referral and recovery in the same direction, so this is a systematic covariate effect, not chance.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity asks whether results extend to other patients and settings. A covariate that distorts the treatment comparison inside the study threatens internal validity, whether the results are correct for the patients studied.

questions.q: Histamine is a mediator of inflammation in patients with allergic rhinitis (“hay fever”). Based on this fact, which of the following is true?
opts: Drugs that block the effects of histamines will relieve symptoms.

This states as fact what is only a hypothesis. Knowing histamine mediates inflammation makes blocking it a promising idea, but whether blocking it actually relieves symptoms must be tested in people who have hay fever.
A fall in histamine levels in the nose is a reliable marker of clinical success.

A fall in nasal histamine is an intermediate biologic outcome, and such measures are not shown to be reliable markers of clinical success. What matters to patients is relief of symptoms such as itchy nose, sneezing and congestion, which must be measured directly.
Antihistamines may be effective, and their effects on symptoms (e.g., itchy nose, sneezing, and congestion) should be studied in patients with allergic rhinitis.

Correct. The fact that histamine mediates inflammation leads to a promising hypothesis that antihistamines may work, but it must be tested. Their effects on symptoms such as itchy nose, sneezing and congestion should be studied in patients with allergic rhinitis.
Other mediators are not important.
This assumes more than the fact given. Histamine is only one of many mediators of inflammation in hay fever, so other mediators may well matter to the symptoms.
If laboratory studies of disease are convincing, clinical research is unnecessary.

Convincing laboratory findings can suggest a hypothesis, but they do not show that patients benefit. The hypothesis still needs to be tested in people with the disease, so clinical research remains necessary.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about samples of populations is incorrect?
opts: Samples of populations may have characteristics that differ from the population even though correct sampling procedures were followed.

This statement is true, so it is not the incorrect one. Even when correct sampling procedures are followed, a sample can differ from its population by chance, which is random variation producing results that differ from the truth.
Samples of populations are the only feasible way of studying the population.

This statement is true, so it is not the incorrect one. A population is all the people in a defined setting, which is generally impractical to study in full, so a subset of it, a sample, is what gets studied.
When populations are correctly sampled, external validity is ensured.

Correct: this is the incorrect statement. Sampling a population correctly does not ensure external validity, because samples can misrepresent the population by chance, especially small ones. External validity, whether results hold in other clinical settings, is rarely determined from a single study.
Samples of populations should be selected in a way that every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen.

This statement is true, so it is not the incorrect one. In a random sample each individual has an equal chance of being selected, which is what keeps selection from systematically favoring some members of the population.

questions.q: You are making a treatment decision with a 72-year-old man with colon cancer. You are aware of several good studies that have shown that a certain drug combination prolongs the life of patients with colon cancer. However, all the patients in these studies were much younger. Which of the statements below is correct?
opts: Given these studies, the decision about this treatment is a matter of personal judgment.

Correct. Applying results from younger patients to a 72-year-old is generalizing beyond the people studied, which is external validity. It is a matter of personal judgment informed by whatever is known about whether older patients respond as younger ones do; generalizability is rarely settled by a single study.
Relying on these studies for your patient is called internal validity.

Relying on studies of other kinds of patients is a question of external validity, also called generalizability. Internal validity is the degree to which results are correct for the sample of patients who were actually studied.
The results in these studies are affected by chance but not bias.

Chance and bias can both affect how correct the results are for the patients studied. Chance is random variation and bias is systematic error, and the two can coexist, so a study cannot be assumed free of bias.

questions.q: A study was done to determine whether regular exercise lowers the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). An exercise program was offered to employees of a factory, and the rates of subsequent coronary events were compared in employees who volunteered for the program and those who did not volunteer. The development of CHD was determined by means of regular voluntary checkups, including a careful history, an electrocardiogram, and a review of routine health records. Surprisingly, the members of the exercise group developed higher rates of CHD even though fewer of them smoked cigarettes. This result is least likely to be explained by which of the following?
opts: The volunteers did not actually increase their exercise and the amount of exercise was the same in the two groups.

Correct: this is the least likely explanation. If volunteers exercised no more than nonvolunteers, exercise could not account for a difference in coronary heart disease. The other explanations involve group differences or unequal detection of the outcome, which can produce the finding.
The volunteers were at higher risk for developing CHD than those not volunteering before the study began.

This is a likely explanation, so it is not the least likely one. If volunteers were at higher risk before the study began, the groups differed in more than the exercise program, which is selection bias, and it could produce higher rates in the exercise group.
Volunteers got more checkups, and silent myocardial infarctions were, therefore, more likely to have been diagnosed in the exercise group.

This is a likely explanation, so it is not the least likely one. Volunteers had more checkups, so silent myocardial infarctions were more likely to be found in them; the outcome was detected unequally between groups, which is measurement bias.

questions.q: Ventricular premature depolarizations are associated with an increased risk of sudden death from a fatal arrhythmia, especially in people with other evidence of heart disease. You have read there is a new drug for ventricular premature depolarizations. What is the most important thing you would like to know about the drug before prescribing it to a patient?
opts: The drug's mechanism of action.
A mechanism of action explains how a drug might work, but it does not show that patients benefit. What matters for prescribing is whether the drug changes the clinical outcome, here sudden death.
How well the drug prevents ventricular premature depolarizations in people using the drug compared to those who do not use the drug.

Suppressing ventricular premature depolarizations is an intermediate biologic outcome, and it can be an unreliable marker of the clinical outcome. Some arrhythmia-suppressing drugs have actually increased the rate of sudden death, so this result alone does not show benefit.
The rate of sudden death in similar people who do and do not take the drug.

Correct. The drug's effect on mortality is the most important thing to determine, so the rate of sudden death in similar people who do and do not take it is what you want. A drug can improve an intermediate biologic outcome yet still increase sudden death.

questions.q:
Because reports suggested estrogens increase the risk of clotting, a study compared the frequency of oral contraceptive use among women admitted to a hospital with thrombophlebitis and a group of women admitted for other reasons. Medical records were reviewed for indication of oral contraceptive use in the two groups. Women with thrombophlebitis were found to have been using oral contraceptives more frequently than the women admitted for other reasons.

Women with thrombophlebitis may have reported the use of contraceptives more completely than women without thrombophlebitis because they remembered hearing of the association.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias concerns how the compared groups were assembled. The concern here is that women with thrombophlebitis remembered and reported contraceptive use more completely, which is a problem in how exposure information was obtained.
Measurement bias

Correct. Asking people about a past exposure relies on memory, and recall bias occurs when those with the illness recall exposures they think are related to it more completely. That makes the exposure measured unequally in the two groups, so it is measurement bias.
Confounding

Confounding needs a covariate associated with both the exposure and the outcome. Fuller recall by women who are ill is not a separate factor tied to both; it is an error in obtaining the exposure information.
Chance

Chance is random variation with no consistent direction. Women with the illness reporting contraceptive use more completely pushes the results in one direction, which is a systematic error rather than chance.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity asks whether the findings apply to other patients and settings. More complete reporting by ill women distorts the results for the women studied, which is a threat to internal validity.

questions.q:
Because reports suggested estrogens increase the risk of clotting, a study compared the frequency of oral contraceptive use among women admitted to a hospital with thrombophlebitis and a group of women admitted for other reasons. Medical records were reviewed for indication of oral contraceptive use in the two groups. Women with thrombophlebitis were found to have been using oral contraceptives more frequently than the women admitted for other reasons.

Doctors may have questioned women with thrombophlebitis more carefully about contraceptive use than they did those without thrombophlebitis (and recorded the information more carefully in the medical record) because they were aware that estrogen could cause clotting.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias concerns how the groups were assembled. Here the groups already exist; the problem is that clinicians asked about and recorded contraceptive use more carefully in women with thrombophlebitis, which is unequal measurement of exposure.
Measurement bias

Correct. Measurement bias occurs when information is not obtained the same way in both groups. Clinicians who knew estrogen can cause clotting questioned and recorded contraceptive use more carefully in women with thrombophlebitis, so exposure was measured unequally.
Confounding

Confounding requires a covariate linked to both exposure and outcome. More careful questioning by doctors is not such a covariate; it is a difference in how the exposure information was collected and recorded.
Chance

Chance is random variation with no consistent direction. Doctors questioning and recording more carefully in only one group systematically inflates the reported exposure in that group, which is bias rather than chance.
External validity (generalizability)
External validity is about whether results extend to other patients and settings. Unequal questioning affects whether the results are correct for the women studied, which is internal validity.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 24; 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 1.13

questions.q:
Because reports suggested estrogens increase the risk of clotting, a study compared the frequency of oral contraceptive use among women admitted to a hospital with thrombophlebitis and a group of women admitted for other reasons. Medical records were reviewed for indication of oral contraceptive use in the two groups. Women with thrombophlebitis were found to have been using oral contraceptives more frequently than the women admitted for other reasons.

The number of women in the study was small.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Selection bias is a systematic difference in how groups were assembled. A small number of women does not by itself make the groups differ systematically; it makes the observed difference more likely to arise by random variation, which is chance.
Measurement bias

Measurement bias is a systematic error in how exposure or outcome is measured. The number of women in the study has no bearing on how contraceptive use was measured; small numbers threaten the result through random variation.
Confounding

Confounding requires a covariate tied to both exposure and outcome. Small size does not identify any such covariate; it raises the possibility that a difference between groups arose by random variation.
Chance

Correct. Chance is random variation producing conclusions that differ from the true results, and small numbers of participants increase the possibility that chance accounts for a difference between groups. Statistical analysis can estimate the role of chance.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity concerns whether results apply to other patients and settings. Having few participants raises doubt about whether the observed difference is real even for the women studied, which is a problem of chance.

questions.q:
Because reports suggested estrogens increase the risk of clotting, a study compared the frequency of oral contraceptive use among women admitted to a hospital with thrombophlebitis and a group of women admitted for other reasons. Medical records were reviewed for indication of oral contraceptive use in the two groups. Women with thrombophlebitis were found to have been using oral contraceptives more frequently than the women admitted for other reasons.

The women with thrombophlebitis were admitted to the hospital by doctors working in different neighborhoods than the physicians of those that did not have thrombophlebitis.

Which response best represents the corresponding threat to validity?
opts: Selection bias

Correct. Selection bias occurs when compared groups differ in more than the focus of the study. Women admitted by doctors in different neighborhoods likely differ in socioeconomic and other characteristics related to health outcomes, so the groups were not comparable to begin with.
Measurement bias

Measurement bias comes from how exposure or outcome is measured. Nothing here says contraceptive use was recorded differently; the statement describes who came to be in each group through admission by doctors in different neighborhoods.
Confounding

Confounding is a covariate whose effect cannot be separated from the exposure's effect at analysis. The statement does not name a covariate tied to both contraceptive use and thrombophlebitis; it describes how the two groups came to be assembled, which is selection.
Chance

Chance is random variation without a consistent direction. Groups drawn from different neighborhoods differ systematically in characteristics related to health, so this is a bias in the groups, not random variation.
External validity (generalizability)

External validity asks whether results extend to other patients and settings. Groups that differ before the comparison begins threaten whether the results are correct for the women studied, which is internal validity.

questions.q: A study was conducted of bladder cancer cases in men. Cancer registries report 40 new cases of bladder cancer per 100,000 men per year. Cases were from a complete count of all patients who developed bladder cancer in several regions of the United States, and the number of men at risk was estimated from the census data in those regions. Which rate is this an example of?
opts: Point prevalence
That is wrong: point prevalence counts existing cases at one moment, while a cancer registry counts new cases arising over a year, so the numerator here is new diagnoses, not cases already present.
Incidence density

Correct. Registries count new cases over a year in a dynamic population, where men are constantly entering and leaving the census population, so the denominator is person-time and the rate is an incidence density.
Period prevalence
That is wrong: period prevalence counts all cases present during a span of time, including old ones, but a registry rate of new bladder cancers per year counts only cases that newly developed.
Cumulative incidence

That is wrong: cumulative incidence needs a group of fixed size followed over time, and men in several regions (estimated from census data) come and go, so a fixed-size denominator does not exist here.
Complication rate

That is wrong: a complication rate describes untoward events in patients who already have a condition or procedure, whereas this denominator is all men at risk in the regions and the events are first diagnoses, which makes it an incidence measure.

questions.q: You are reading a study of the prevalence of uterine cervix infections and want to decide if the study is scientifically sound. Which of the following is not important?
opts: Participants are followed up for a sufficient period of time for infection to occur.

Correct. This is the item that is not important, because a prevalence study is a snapshot: it counts existing cases at a single point in time and does not follow anyone forward, so a follow-up period is not part of its design.
The study is done on a representative sample of the population.

This is important, so it is not the answer: a prevalence study should draw a representative sample from the defined population, because an unrepresentative sample would give a prevalence that does not apply to that population.
All members of the population are women.

This is important, so it is not the answer: the population at risk should include only people who can have the condition, and cervical infection can occur only in women, so including men would dilute the prevalence.
Cervical infection is clearly defined.
This is important, so it is not the answer: case definition strongly affects how many cases are counted, so a prevalence study must define cervical infection clearly before anyone is counted.
The study is done on a sample from a defined population.
This is important, so it is not the answer: a prevalence study begins with a defined population from which the sample is drawn, so the result can be applied to that population.

questions.q: A probability sample of a defined population:
opts: Is invalidated by oversampling.

That is wrong: a probability sample gives every person a known chance of selection, not necessarily an equal one, and it is the design used when subgroups need extra representation, so deliberately taking more people from a subgroup does not invalidate it.
Is inferior to a random sample.

That is wrong: a random sample is simply the special case of a probability sample in which every person has an equal chance, so a probability sample is not inferior to it and can be the better choice when subgroups such as age or ethnicity are studied.
Is not representative of the population.

That is wrong: because every person has a known probability of being selected, a probability sample is designed to represent the population it was drawn from, and it does so in the long run when enough people are sampled.
Results in a representative sample of the population only if there are enough people in the sample.
Correct. A random or probability sample is representative of the population sampled in the long run, so the sample must be large enough for chance variation to average out.

questions.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) would like to know the average duration of her disease. You cannot find a study that directly answers that question. However, other studies show a prevalence of 1.5%, and annual incidence of 50/100,000. These rates have been stable. On average, how many years does the disease persist?
opts: Dividing 1.5% by 50 per 100,000 per year (0.015 / 0.0005) gives 30, not 15. A duration of 15 years would need a prevalence of only 0.75% at the same incidence.
The ratio 0.015 / 0.0005 is 30 years, not 25. A duration of 25 years would need a prevalence of 1.25% at this incidence, which is not what the studies show.
Correct. In a steady state, prevalence equals incidence times average duration, so duration = prevalence / incidence = 0.015 / (50 / 100,000 per year) = 30 years.
That is wrong: 33 years would need a prevalence of about 1.65% at this incidence. The correct ratio 0.015 / 0.0005 is exactly 30, and 33 does not come from a valid rearrangement of these numbers.

That is wrong: 50 is simply the incidence figure (per 100,000 per year) copied as the answer. A 50-year duration would need a prevalence of 2.5%, and the actual ratio of 1.5% to 0.05% per year is 30 years.

questions.q: Which of the following studies is not a cohort study?
opts: The proportion of patients with stomach cancer who survive 5 years

This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: patients with stomach cancer form a group with a shared characteristic (the disease) who are followed forward in time to see how many are alive at 5 years.
The risk of developing diabetes mellitus in children according to their weight
This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: children grouped by weight (the exposure) and followed forward for the development of diabetes is the classic exposure-defined cohort design.
Complications of influenza vaccine among children vaccinated in 2011
This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: children vaccinated in 2011 share a characteristic (receiving an intervention at a similar time) and are followed forward for complications.
The earlier course of disease in a group of patients now under care in a clinic

Correct. A cohort is a group with a common characteristic assembled at a similar point, such as disease onset, and followed forward; patients already under care at varied stages, whose earlier course is reviewed, share no common starting point, so this is not a cohort study.
Patients admitted to an intensive care unit and followed up for whether they are still alive at the time of hospital discharge
This is a cohort study, so it is not the answer: admission to the intensive care unit is the shared starting point, and the patients are followed forward to the outcome of being alive at discharge.

questions.q: A sample for a study of incidence of medication errors is obtained by enrolling every 10th patient admitted to a hospital. What kind of sample is this?
opts: Stratified sample

That is wrong: a stratified sample first divides the population into subgroups (such as age or ethnicity) and samples within each, but here there are no subgroups, only a fixed rule based on admission order.
Probability sample

That is wrong: a probability sample requires that each patient have a known chance of selection set by a chance process, and this design describes no random start or other chance mechanism, only a convenient rule tied to the order of arrival.
Convenience sample

Correct, as the best of these choices. Enrolling every 10th admission is a convenient rule with no stated random element or random start (strictly this is systematic sampling, which counts as a probability sample only when the starting point is chosen at random); it might produce a representative sample, but because selection is not by chance it could misrepresent the hospital's patients.
Random sample

That is wrong: in a random sample every patient has an equal chance of being selected by chance, but here selection is fixed by position in the admission order with no random element, so it is not random even if the resulting sample looks representative.
Oversample
That is wrong: an oversample deliberately takes extra people from a subgroup to study it, and nothing in this design targets a subgroup; it is a fixed every-10th rule.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 2.6

questions.q: A study was performed to determine rates of hospital-acquired infection. Participants were 1,000 patients randomly selected from 150 hospitals in 5 countries. Over a 4-month period, surveys were conducted on a single day at each hospital (the date varied by hospital), and medical records were reviewed for that date to determine the presence of hospital-acquired infection. At least one hospital-acquired infection was found in 4% of patients. Which rate is this an example of?
opts: Point prevalence

Correct. Each patient was assessed at a single point in time (one survey day at each hospital), and the proportion with an infection on that day is point prevalence; the survey dates may differ between hospitals.
Complication rate

That is wrong: a complication rate describes untoward events among patients who already have a condition or procedure, whereas this is the share of all sampled patients found to have an infection on the survey day.
Incidence density

That is wrong: incidence density counts new cases over person-time in a changing population, but this survey followed no one over time and counted every infection present on the survey day, not only new ones.
Cumulative incidence
That is wrong: cumulative incidence follows a fixed-size group forward and counts new cases, but here each patient was seen once on a single day with no follow-up.
Period prevalence

That is wrong: period prevalence counts cases present at any time during a defined span, but each person was assessed at only one time point; the four-month spread only reflects that hospitals were surveyed on different dates.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 2.7

questions.q: Cohort studies of children with a first febrile seizure have shown that they have a one in three chance of having another seizure during childhood. What kind of rate is this?
opts: Point prevalence
That is wrong: point prevalence is a snapshot of existing cases at one time, but this one-in-three figure comes from following children forward and counting who has a new seizure.
Cumulative incidence
Correct. The children start as a fixed-size cohort with a first seizure and are followed forward, and the proportion who develop a new event (another seizure) over time is cumulative incidence.
Complication rate

That is wrong: a complication rate describes untoward events in patients undergoing a treatment or procedure, while this is the risk of a repeat event in a fixed cohort followed through childhood, which is cumulative incidence.
Period prevalence
That is wrong: period prevalence counts all existing cases during a span of time in a population, but here a fixed cohort was followed forward to count new recurrences.
Incidence density
That is wrong: incidence density has a person-time denominator for a changing population, whereas this cohort is a fixed group of children with a first seizure and the figure is a simple proportion.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 2.8

questions.q: Which of the following would not increase the observed incidence of disease?
opts: More aggressive efforts to detect the disease
This would increase observed incidence: looking harder for a disease finds cases that would otherwise go unrecognized, so the counted new cases rise even if the true occurrence has not changed.
A true increase in incidence
This would increase observed incidence: if the disease really is occurring more often, more new cases will be counted, and that is the one change that reflects a real difference.
A more sensitive way of detecting the disease
This would increase observed incidence: a more sensitive method identifies more of the people who have the disease, so the number of new cases counted rises with no real change.
A lowering of the threshold for diagnosis of disease
This would increase observed incidence: the case definition affects the frequency counted, and a lower threshold means milder or borderline findings are called disease, adding cases.
Studying a larger sample of the population

Correct. A larger sample only gives an estimate closer to the true incidence by reducing random error; it introduces no systematic difference in how cases are found or defined, so it would not raise the observed incidence.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 2.9

questions.q: A 25-year-old man from Arizona presents to the emergency room with cough, fever, and shortness of breath for the past week. A chest radiograph is consistent with pneumonia. Among the considerations for the source of pneumonia is coccidioidomycosis, a fungus that is common in the deserts of the southwestern United States and in Mexico, but uncommon elsewhere. Which of the following best describes this infection?
opts: Endemic
Correct. Endemic refers to a disease limited by geographic location, and coccidioidomycosis is found mainly in the deserts of the southwestern United States and Mexico.
Pandemic
That is wrong: a pandemic is widespread disease across regions in a given time, which is the opposite of an infection confined to one geographic area.
Incident
That is wrong: incident describes new cases as in incidence, not the geographic pattern of a disease, so it does not describe an infection limited to a region.
Epidemic
That is wrong: an epidemic is a concentration of new cases in a given time, a temporal pattern, whereas a fungus that is steadily common in one geographic area is endemic.
Prevalent
That is wrong: prevalent describes cases existing at a time, a measure of how many have the disease, and does not say that the disease is limited to a geographic area.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 32; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 2.10

questions.q: Twenty-six percent of adults report having experienced back pain lasting at least a day in the prior 3 months. Which of the following best describes this rate?
opts: Cumulative incidence
That is wrong: cumulative incidence counts new cases in a fixed group followed forward, but this survey asks about back pain at any time in the past 3 months, which includes existing cases.
Incidence density
That is wrong: incidence density counts new cases per person-time in a changing population, whereas this is a proportion of adults with pain, not new onsets per person-time.
Point prevalence
That is wrong: point prevalence is a count at a single point in time, but this one covers any pain lasting at least a day over a 3-month window.
Complication rate
That is wrong: a complication rate describes untoward events among patients with a condition or procedure, and back pain in a sample of adults in general is not measured as a complication.
Period prevalence
Correct. The cases existed at any time within a 3-month window, and prevalence measured over a specified time period, including anyone who had pain at any point in it, is period prevalence.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 2.11

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a “dynamic population”?
opts: It is rapidly increasing in size.
That is wrong: a dynamic population does not have to be growing; entries by birth or moving in can be balanced by deaths and moving out, and size is not what makes it dynamic.
It is uniquely suited for cohort studies.
That is wrong: cohort studies follow a group of fixed size, so a population that is continually changing membership is not suited to them; incidence density is used for dynamic populations.
People are continually entering and leaving the population.
Correct. A dynamic population has people continually entering (born, moving in) and leaving (dying, moving out), which is why incidence in it is measured in person-time.
It is the basis for measuring cumulative incidence.
That is wrong: cumulative incidence needs a group of fixed size followed over time, whereas a dynamic population is the setting for incidence density, with a person-time denominator.
It is the best kind of population for a random sample.
That is wrong: whether a population is dynamic has no bearing on random sampling; a random sample only requires that each person have an equal chance of selection.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 2.12

questions.q: During a clinic visit, a mother wonders if her newborn could develop scoliosis (a deformity of the spine that becomes apparent after birth, most often in adolescence). To provide this estimate you review the literature. Which cohort would be most appropriate to answer her question?
opts: Children who were referred to an orthopedic surgeon for treatment
That is wrong: children referred to an orthopedic surgeon are a selected group already known to have a problem, so following them cannot show how likely a newborn is to develop scoliosis.
Children born in North Carolina in 2012 and examined for scoliosis until they are adults

Correct. A cohort is a group with a common starting characteristic followed forward, and children born in the same place and year and examined until adulthood show how often scoliosis develops over time.
Children who were found to have scoliosis in a survey of children in North Carolina

That is wrong: children already found to have scoliosis are existing cases at one time, which describes prevalence, and this group cannot estimate the chance that a newborn will develop the condition.
Children who have scoliosis and are available for study
That is wrong: children who have scoliosis and are available form a convenience sample of existing cases, with no followed-forward group of unaffected children to show new onset.
Children who were randomly sampled from the population of North Carolina in the spring of 2012
That is wrong: a random sample of children at one point in spring 2012 is a snapshot that estimates prevalence, not a group followed forward to see new cases develop.

questions.q: Which of the following are prevalence studies especially useful for?
opts: Describing the incidence of disease
That is wrong: prevalence studies count existing cases at a point in time and do not follow people to see who develops disease, so incidence comes from cohort (incidence) studies.
Studying diseases that resolve rapidly
That is wrong: a disease that resolves quickly leaves few cases at any one moment, so a snapshot finds very little; prevalence studies suit common, longer-lasting conditions.
Estimating the duration of disease
That is wrong: prevalence depends on both how often disease arises and how long it lasts, so a prevalence study by itself cannot give duration without also knowing incidence.
Describing the proportion of people in a defined population with the condition of interest
Correct. A prevalence (cross-sectional) study assesses a defined population for a condition and reports the proportion that has it, which is why it helps plan health services.
Establishing cause and effect
That is wrong: a cross-sectional design is poor for determining cause and effect because exposure and disease are measured together; it is better for generating hypotheses.

questions.q: Last year, 800,000 Americans died of heart disease or stoke. Which of the following best describes this statistic?
opts: Incidence density
That is wrong: incidence density is new cases divided by person-time, and 800,000 deaths is only a count with no person-time denominator and no population at risk.
Point prevalence
That is wrong: point prevalence is a proportion of a group with a condition at one time, and a bare count of deaths does not have a group of people examined as its denominator.
Cumulative incidence
That is wrong: cumulative incidence is new cases divided by a fixed-size group at risk, and a bare count of 800,000 deaths has no denominator to express a fraction.
Period prevalence
That is wrong: period prevalence is a proportion of a group with the condition over a span, and here only a number of deaths is given, with no population it is a fraction of.
None of the above
Correct. A rate compares events to a population over a time period, so a raw count of 800,000 deaths without a denominator is not a rate and fits none of the incidence or prevalence measures.

questions.q:
Deep tendon reflex grade 0 (no response), 1+ (somewhat diminished), 2+ (normal), 3+ (brisker than average), and 4+ (very brisk).

Which is the most appropriate term for this type of data?
opts: Interval—Continuous

Reflex grades are ordered categories, not measurements on a scale with equal steps, so this is not interval data. Interval data needs defined, equal intervals between values, and nothing says the gap from 1+ to 2+ equals the gap from 3+ to 4+; continuous data such as weight or blood pressure also takes any value on a continuum.
Dichotomous
Dichotomous data has only two categories (yes/no, present/absent). Reflex grading has five ordered levels from 0 to 4+, so it is more than two categories and is ordinal rather than dichotomous.
Nominal

Nominal data is categories without any specified order, such as blood type or eye color. Reflex grades run from absent through normal to very brisk, so the categories have a built-in order, which makes them ordinal rather than nominal.
Ordinal

Correct. Ordinal data has an order to the categories but no defined intervals between them. Reflex grades 0 to 4+ rank from no response to very brisk, so you know which is more or less, but not by how much (pitting edema 1+ to 4+ and cancer stages I to IV are the same kind of data).
Interval—Discrete

Interval-discrete data has defined, equal intervals and takes only specific values, such as a count of children or heart attacks. Reflex grades are ranked labels with no defined equal spacing between grades, so they are ordinal and not interval of any kind.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 50; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 51; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 3.1

questions.q:
Cancer recurrent/not recurrent 5 years after initial treatment.

Which is the most appropriate term for this type of data?
opts: Interval—Continuous

Interval-continuous data has ordered values with equal intervals that can fall anywhere on a continuum, like blood pressure or weight. Recurrent versus not recurrent is just two categories with no numeric scale, so it cannot be interval data.
Dichotomous
Correct. Dichotomous data is nominal data divided into exactly two categories (yes/no, present/absent). Cancer that has or has not recurred at 5 years fits that pattern.
Nominal

Nominal is the broader family of unordered categories such as blood type or eye color, and dichotomous data is a subtype of it. Because this outcome has only two categories, the more specific and most appropriate term is dichotomous.
Ordinal

Ordinal data has three or more categories with a meaningful rank, such as cancer stage I to IV. Recurrent versus not recurrent is a two-category present/absent outcome, so it is dichotomous, not ordinal.
Interval—Discrete

Interval-discrete data is a count that takes specific numeric values with equal intervals, such as the number of heart attacks. A yes/no outcome about recurrence is a category, not a count, so it is dichotomous.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 49; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 3.2

questions.q:
Serum sodium 139 mg/dL.

Which is the most appropriate term for this type of data?
opts: Interval—Continuous

Correct. A serum sodium value is a measurement on a numeric scale with equal intervals that can fall anywhere along a continuum, limited only by the precision of the laboratory method. That is interval-continuous data, like blood pressure and weight.
Dichotomous

Dichotomous data has just two categories, such as present or absent. A serum sodium of 139 is a numeric value on a scale, not one of two categories (a normal versus abnormal label would be dichotomous, but the raw value is not).
Nominal
Nominal data sorts things into unordered categories, such as blood type. A serum sodium is a number with a defined order and equal intervals, so it is interval data, not nominal.
Ordinal

Ordinal data ranks categories without defined intervals, such as edema graded 1+ to 4+. A sodium level is reported as an exact number on a scale with equal steps between values, which makes it interval data instead.
Interval—Discrete

Interval-discrete data can take only specific values, typically counts such as the number of children. Sodium is not counted; it can take any value on a continuum, limited only by measurement precision, so it is continuous rather than discrete.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 51; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 3.3

questions.q:
Three seizures per month.

Which is the most appropriate term for this type of data?
opts: Interval—Continuous

Continuous data can take any value along a continuum, such as weight, allowing fractions limited only by precision. A number of seizures is a whole-number count (you cannot have 2.5 seizures), so it is discrete.
Dichotomous
Dichotomous data has only two categories. Three seizures per month is a count that can be 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on, not a yes/no category, so it is not dichotomous.
Nominal
Nominal data is unordered categories, such as eye color. A number of seizures per month is numeric, with equal steps between counts, so it is interval data and not nominal.
Ordinal

Ordinal data ranks categories with no defined interval between them, such as edema grades. Seizure counts have exact, equal intervals (three is exactly one more than two), so they are interval data rather than ordinal.
Interval—Discrete

Correct. Discrete interval data takes only specific values and has equal intervals; counts such as the number of children or heart attacks are the examples. Three seizures per month is a count, so it is interval-discrete.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 51; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 3.4

questions.q:
Causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding: duodenal ulcer, gastritis, esophageal, or other varices.

Which is the most appropriate term for this type of data?
opts: Interval—Continuous
Interval-continuous data is numeric, with equal intervals along a continuum. The cause of bleeding is a named category (ulcer, gastritis, varices), not a number, so it cannot be interval data.
Dichotomous
Dichotomous data has exactly two categories. This list has several causes (duodenal ulcer, gastritis, varices, other), so it is nominal with more than two categories rather than dichotomous.
Nominal
Correct. Nominal data is categories without a specified order, like blood type or eye color. Duodenal ulcer, gastritis and varices are labels with no ranking, so the cause of bleeding is nominal.
Ordinal

Ordinal data has categories with a meaningful order, such as cancer stage. Nothing ranks a duodenal ulcer above or below gastritis or varices, so these unordered causes are nominal rather than ordinal.
Interval—Discrete
Interval-discrete data is a count that takes specific numeric values with equal intervals. The causes of bleeding are named categories, not counts, so the data is nominal.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 49; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 3.5

questions.q: When it is not possible to verify measurement of a phenomenon, such as itching, by the physical senses, which of the following can be said about its validity?
opts: It is questionable, and one should rely on “hard” measures such as laboratory tests.

Validity can be pursued even without physical verification, and hard laboratory measures are not the only valid ones. Structured questions and pain scales are used for subjective symptoms, and content, criterion and construct validity are strategies for assessing them.
It can be established by showing that the same value is obtained when the measurement is repeated by many different observers at different times.

Getting the same value from many observers at different times shows reliability (consistency, reproducibility). A measure can be consistent yet consistently wrong, so agreement between observers does not show that it measures what it should.
It can be supported by showing that the measurement is related to other measures of phenomena such as the presence of diseases that are known to cause itching.

Correct. Showing that the measure is related to other measures believed to be part of the same phenomenon, such as diseases known to cause itching, supports validity without physical verification. That approach is described as construct validity.
It can be established by showing that measurement results in a broad range of values.

A broad range of values reflects variation, not accuracy, and does nothing to show the measure captures the phenomenon it is meant to. If repeated measurements of the same thing spread widely, that points to poor reliability, not established validity.
It cannot be established.

Validity of a subjective measure can be supported even when the senses cannot verify it. Content validity, criterion validity and construct validity are the strategies used when physical verification is not possible, so saying it cannot be established is wrong.

questions.q: A physician or nurse measures a patient's heart rate by feeling the pulse for 10 seconds each time she comes to clinic. The rates might differ from visit to visit because of all the following except:
opts: The pulse rate varies among patients.

Correct (this is the exception). Differences in pulse among different patients are inter-patient variation, which does not explain why one patient's readings differ from visit to visit. The question is about variation within a single patient.
The patient has a different pulse rate at different times.
This does explain visit-to-visit differences. A person's pulse changes with the time of day, position and stress, which is true biologic (intra-patient) variation.
The measurement may misrepresent the true pulse by chance because of the brief period of observation.
This does explain differences. Feeling the pulse for only 10 seconds gives a short sample, so chance can make the estimate too high or too low, which is random measurement error.
The physician and nurse use different techniques (e.g., different degrees of pressure on the pulse).
This does explain differences. Different techniques or pressures between examiners are interobserver variation, a measurement source of variation that affects reliability.
An effective treatment was begun between visits.

This does explain differences. Within-patient change can reflect a true biologic change, and a treatment that acts on the patient's condition could change the pulse between visits, so it is a legitimate reason for the readings to differ.

questions.q: “Abnormal” is commonly defined by all of the following except:
opts: The level at which treatment has been shown to be effective
Treatment effectiveness is a commonly used way to define abnormal: values are called abnormal when lowering them has been shown to help. So this is a real definition and not the exception.
The level at which death rate is increased

A level at which the death rate rises is a common definition of abnormal, because abnormal is best defined in relation to values known to be associated with disease, disability or death. So this is not the exception.
Statistically unusual values

Statistically unusual values (far from the average, for example beyond 2 standard deviations) are commonly used to define abnormal, although statistical abnormality does not always mean clinical abnormality. So this is a real definition and not the exception.
The level at which there is an increased risk of symptoms
A level at which the risk of symptoms rises is a common definition of abnormal, since abnormality is defined by association with disease or disability. So this is not the exception.
Values that do not correspond to a normal distribution

Correct (this is the exception). Abnormal is not defined by whether values fit a normal distribution. Clinical measurements do not necessarily follow a normal distribution (the normal curve is a mathematical model), so failing to match its shape says nothing about being abnormal.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 73; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 75; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 77; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 3.8

questions.q: All of the following statements are true except:
opts: The normal distribution describes the distribution of most naturally occurring phenomena.

Correct (this is the false statement). The normal curve is a mathematical model, not a description of what is actually measured, and naturally occurring clinical measurements may or may not resemble it. Skewed examples include neutrophil counts and the United States vitamin D levels.
The normal distribution includes 2.5% of people in each tail of the distribution (beyond 2 standard deviations from the mean).

This is true. In a normal distribution about 95% of values fall within 2 standard deviations of the mean, leaving roughly 5% outside, split evenly between the two tails (about 2.5% in each), so it is not the false statement.
The normal distribution is unimodal and symmetrical.
This is true. The normal (Gaussian, bell) curve has one peak and is symmetrical around it, with the mean, median and mode at the same point, so it is not the false statement.
The normal distribution is the most common basis for defining abnormal laboratory tests measured on interval scales.

This is true. Laboratory values measured on interval scales are commonly called abnormal when they are statistically unusual, meaning far into the tails of the normal curve, so this statement is accurate and is not the exception.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 72; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 73; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 3.9

questions.q: You see a new patient who is a 45-year-old man who presents to the clinic to establish care. He has not been seen for medical care for the last 10 years. He is on no medications and he has no known health problems. He does not use tobacco products, alcohol, or recreational drugs. He is 7 kg overweight. His blood pressure is elevated at 151/95. Which of the following statements is least correct?
opts: The patient is likely to have a lower blood pressure if measured again this visit.

This is true, so it is not the least correct statement. An unusually high reading tends to be followed by one closer to the average (regression to the mean), and settling of anxiety during the visit can also lower it.
The patient is likely to have a lower blood pressure if measured at home.

This is true, so it is not the least correct statement. Blood pressure measured in the clinic can be raised by the white coat phenomenon, so readings taken at home are often lower and give a better picture of usual pressure.
The elevated blood pressure could be influenced by chance.

This is true, so it is not the least correct statement. Any single reading includes random variation from biologic fluctuation and measurement error, so chance can make one measurement look higher than the patient's usual blood pressure.
The patient should be given a prescription for an antihypertensive to lower his risk of coronary heart disease.

Correct (this is the least correct statement). A single elevated reading is not enough to label someone hypertensive and start treatment. Abnormal tests should be confirmed by repeating them, since chance, technique or the white coat effect can raise one reading and an unusually high reading tends to be followed by a lower one (regression to the mean); treatment fits once the diagnosis is confirmed.

questions.q:
Figure 3.13 shows the distribution of vitamin D for two populations of randomly selected black participants at different latitudes: 497 participants from a city in the United States (Chicago; 41 degrees latitude; purple curve) and 459 participate from a city in Ghana (Kumasi, 6 degrees latitude, orange curve).

Which statement about central tendency is correct for the U.S. distribution?
opts: Mean, median, and mode are the same

Mean, median and mode coincide in a symmetrical curve such as the normal distribution, as roughly seen for the Ghana sample. The United States curve has a long tail toward high values, so the three measures are pulled apart.
Mode < median < mean

Correct. The United States curve peaks at low values and has a long right tail (right skew). The mode is at the peak, the mean is dragged toward the tail by the high values, and the median lies between them, so mode is less than median, which is less than mean.
Mode < mean < median

This ordering puts the median above the mean. In a right-skewed curve the mean is pulled furthest toward the long tail by the extreme values, so the mean is the largest and the median sits between the mode and mean.
Mode > median > mean

This ordering (mode highest, mean lowest) would fit a left-skewed curve, with the long tail toward low values. The United States curve has its tail toward high values, so the mode is the smallest and the mean the largest.
Mode > mean > median

This ordering puts the median as the smallest of the three, which does not match a single-peaked skewed curve like this one, where the median falls between the mode and the mean. Here the mode is lowest, not highest.

Figure 3.13 shows the distribution of vitamin D for two populations of randomly selected black participants at different latitudes: 497 participants from a city in the United States (Chicago; 41 degrees latitude; purple curve) and 459 participate from a city in Ghana (Kumasi, 6 degrees latitude, orange curve).

Which statement about dispersion is most correct
opts: The range is the best way to describe the Ghana sample.
Range depends only on the two extreme values, so it is easily distorted by outliers and is not the best summary. The Ghana sample is roughly normal, so standard deviation describes its spread well.
Standard deviation is the best way to describe the U.S. sample.

Standard deviation is best suited to a roughly normal (symmetrical) distribution. The United States curve is skewed, so the standard deviation does not describe its dispersion accurately, which makes it a poor choice for that sample.
Ninety-five percent of the vitamin D levels will fall within about 2 standard deviations of the mean for the Ghana sample.

Correct. The Ghana sample is approximately normally distributed, and in a normal distribution about 95% of values fall within 2 standard deviations of the mean (about two-thirds fall within 1 standard deviation).
The standard deviation is about 15 ng/mL for the Ghana sample.

This value is too large for the Ghana curve. Its values run only from about 10 to 50, and about 7 is the approximate standard deviation, so a standard deviation of 15 would put the 2-standard-deviation band well beyond the plotted values.

Figure 3.14 compares fetal heart rates measured by electronic monitoring (white middle bar), to measurements by hospital staff in three different circumstances: when fetal heart rate of beats per minute by electronic monitoring was normal (130–150), low (<130), and high (>150).

The distribution of hospital staff measurements around the electronic monitor measurement in Panel A of Figure 3.14 could be due to:
opts: Chance

Chance does contribute, since the errors fall about equally above and below the true value, but it is not the only source. Different staff members making the readings (interobserver variability) can also spread the results, so chance alone is incomplete.
Interobserver variability

Interobserver variability plausibly contributes, since different staff measure differently, but it is not the only source. The errors are evenly balanced on both sides of the monitor value, which is the signature of random chance, so this alone is incomplete.
Biased preference for normal results

A biased preference for normal results would push the errors mostly in one direction, toward the normal range. In this panel the monitor rate was already normal and errors fall evenly on both sides, so bias is not what the shape shows, and it could not be the only explanation.
A and B

Correct. Errors spread about equally above and below the monitor value, which is random measurement error (chance, equal probability of being above or below the true value). Different staff taking the readings (interobserver variability) can add to the spread. No consistent one-sided shift is seen.
A and C

This adds a biased preference for normal results. When the monitor value is normal, a preference for normal results would not shift the readings in one direction, and the errors are evenly balanced, so no systematic bias is shown; interobserver variability is also left out.
B and C

This adds a biased preference for normal results, but the errors fall evenly on both sides of the monitor value rather than leaning one way, so bias is not shown here. It also leaves out chance, which is the main reason for the balanced scatter.
A, B, and C

This includes biased preference for normal results, which would produce a consistent shift of the readings in one direction. Here the errors are evenly balanced above and below the monitor value, so a systematic bias is not what the panel shows.

The distribution of hospital staff measurements around the electronic monitor measurement in Panel B of Figure 3.14 could be due to:
opts: Chance

Chance does contribute to scatter, but it cannot explain a shift mostly to one side. When the monitor rate was low, staff readings ran mostly above the true value, so chance alone is incomplete; a systematic tilt and observer differences also apply.
Interobserver variability

Interobserver variability does contribute, since different staff measure differently, but it does not by itself explain readings that lean consistently in one direction. Chance and a systematic preference for normal values also play a part.
Biased preference for normal results

A biased preference for normal results explains the shift: readings above the low monitor rate were recorded as closer to normal. But not every reading is identical, and the remaining spread reflects chance and different observers, so bias alone is incomplete.
A and B

This covers chance and interobserver variability, which explain the spread, but leaves out the consistent lean toward higher readings. That one-sided shift is systematic error, so a biased preference for normal results must be included.
A and C

This includes chance and bias but leaves out interobserver variability. Because different staff members took the measurements and the values are not all the same, differences between observers also contribute to the spread.
B and C

This includes interobserver variability and bias but leaves out chance. Readings that are not all identical also reflect random measurement error, which has equal probability of being above or below the true value.
A, B, and C

Correct. Staff readings lean to the right, overestimating the low monitor rates and recording them closer to normal. That is systematic error (bias), a flaw in the process. The remaining scatter reflects chance and variation between observers, so all three apply.

A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

What is the sensitivity of facial pain for sinusitis in this study?
opts: That is 49/128, the positive predictive value: the share of patients with facial pain who actually had sinusitis. Sensitivity divides by everyone with the disease (95), not by everyone with a positive test (128).
That figure is 73/152, the specificity: the share of patients without sinusitis who lacked facial pain. Sensitivity instead divides the true positives by all 95 patients with disease: 49/95 = 52%.

Correct. Sensitivity is the probability that a person with disease has a positive test: true positives divided by (true positives + false negatives). Here 49 of the 95 patients with sinusitis had facial pain, so 49/95 = 52%.

That is 73/119, the negative predictive value: the share of patients without facial pain who truly did not have sinusitis. Sensitivity uses only the 95 patients with disease as its denominator, giving 49/95 = 52%.

A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

What is the specificity?
opts: That is 49/128, the positive predictive value (also close to the overall prevalence of 95/247). Specificity looks only at the 152 patients WITHOUT sinusitis and asks how many lacked facial pain: 73/152.

Correct. Specificity is the probability that a person without disease has a negative test: true negatives divided by (true negatives + false positives). Of the 152 patients without sinusitis, 79 had facial pain (false positives), leaving 152 - 79 = 73 true negatives, and 73/152 = 48%.
That is 49/95, the sensitivity (the true positive rate among patients with sinusitis). It also equals 1 minus specificity, roughly 79/152, the false-positive rate. Specificity is 73/152 = 48%.
That is 73/119, the negative predictive value, which divides by all patients with a negative test (119). Specificity divides the 73 true negatives by the 152 patients without disease.

A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

If the doctor thought the patient had sinusitis because the patient had facial pain, for what percent of patients would she be correct?
opts: Correct. This is the positive predictive value: of everyone with a positive test (facial pain), the share who truly have disease. Positives = 49 + 79 = 128, and 49/128 = 38%.

That is 73/152, the specificity, which asks how often patients without sinusitis lack facial pain. The doctor here is starting from a positive finding, so the denominator must be the 128 patients with facial pain.
That is 49/95, the sensitivity, which starts from the 95 patients known to have sinusitis. The doctor is reasoning from the finding to the disease, which is the positive predictive value, 49/128.

That is 73/119, the negative predictive value, which applies when the finding is absent. Here the doctor is judging patients who HAVE facial pain, so the answer is the positive predictive value, 49/128 = 38%.

If the doctor thought the patient did not have sinusitis because the patient did not have facial pain, for what percent of patients would she be correct?
opts: That is 49/128, the positive predictive value, which applies to patients who DO have facial pain. This doctor is reasoning about patients without facial pain, so the negative predictive value (73/119) applies.

That is 73/152, the specificity, whose denominator is the 152 patients without sinusitis. Being correct when facial pain is absent means dividing true negatives by all 119 patients without facial pain.
That is 49/95, the sensitivity, which starts from patients known to have sinusitis. The question starts from the negative test result, so the denominator is the 119 patients without facial pain.
Correct. This is the negative predictive value: of everyone with a negative test (no facial pain), the share who truly are disease free. Negatives = 46 + 73 = 119, and 73/119 = 61%.
