A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

How common was sinusitis in this study?
opts: Correct. Prevalence is the proportion of the studied population that has the disease: 95 patients with sinusitis out of 247 total = 38%. It is not affected by the test result at all.
That is close to the proportion of patients WITHOUT facial pain (119/247, about 48%) and equals the specificity, 73/152. Prevalence is the count with disease over the total: 95/247.
That equals the sensitivity (49/95), and it is also near the proportion of all patients who had facial pain (128/247). Neither is prevalence, which counts only sinusitis cases over the total, 95/247.
That is the negative predictive value, 73/119. Prevalence ignores the test entirely and is the number with disease divided by everyone studied: 95/247 = 38%.

A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

What is the posttest probability of sinusitis in patients with facial pain in this study?
opts: Correct. Facial pain has a positive likelihood ratio of about 1.0 (sensitivity 0.52 divided by 1 minus specificity, which is 0.52 / 0.52), so it does not change the probability: pretest odds 0.61 x 1.0 = posttest odds 0.61, and 0.61/(1 + 0.61) = 38%, the same as the prevalence and the positive predictive value.

That is the specificity (73/152). The posttest probability comes from multiplying the pretest odds by the likelihood ratio and converting back; with a ratio of about 1.0 the probability stays at the pretest 38%, not 48%.
That is the sensitivity (49/95). A positive test raises the probability only if the positive likelihood ratio exceeds 1; here it is about 1.0, so the probability stays at 38%.
That is the negative predictive value, and it also matches the pretest odds of 0.61, which is an intermediate step and not a probability of disease. The posttest probability after facial pain is 38%.

A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

What is the probability of sinusitis in patients assigned a “high probability” by clinicians?
opts: A high-probability clinical impression has a likelihood ratio of 4.7, which is greater than 1, so it must RAISE the probability above the 38% starting point. A value of 10% would require a likelihood ratio of only about 0.2.
About 20% is the result for a LOW probability impression (likelihood ratio 0.4). A ratio of 4.7 moves the 38% pretest probability upward, not down.
About 45% is what a likelihood ratio near 1.4 (an intermediate impression) produces. A ratio of 4.7 is over three times larger and pushes the probability well above that.
Correct. Pretest odds = 0.38/0.62 = 0.61; multiplying by the likelihood ratio of 4.7 gives posttest odds of about 2.9, and 2.9/(1 + 2.9) = 74%, about 75%. The nomogram gives the same answer.
About 90% would need a likelihood ratio of roughly 15, which is well above the 4.7 reported for a high-probability impression. A ratio of 4.7 gives posttest odds of 2.9, or about 74%.

A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

What is the probability of sinusitis in patients assigned an “intermediate probability” by clinicians?
opts: About 10% would require a likelihood ratio of roughly 0.2 (moderate evidence to rule out). An intermediate impression has a ratio near 1.4, which is slightly above 1 and so nudges the probability up from 38%, not down.
About 20% is the result for a LOW probability impression, whose likelihood ratio is 0.4. An intermediate impression has a ratio of 1.4, which does not lower the probability that far.

Correct. An intermediate impression has a likelihood ratio of 1.4, which is indeterminate (0.5 to 2). Pretest odds 0.61 x 1.4 = 0.86, and 0.86/(1 + 0.86) = 46%, about 45%: little change from the 38% starting point.
About 75% is the result for a HIGH probability impression (likelihood ratio 4.7). A ratio of only 1.4 in the indeterminate range barely changes the pretest probability.
About 90% would require a likelihood ratio of about 15, in the strong rule-in range (above 10). An intermediate impression has a ratio of 1.4, which is indeterminate.

A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

What is the probability of sinusitis in patients assigned a “low probability” by clinicians?
opts: About 10% would require a likelihood ratio of roughly 0.2 (moderate evidence to rule out). A low-probability impression has a ratio of 0.4, which is only weak evidence to rule out, leaving about 20%.

Correct. A low-probability impression has a likelihood ratio of 0.4 (weak evidence to rule out, 0.2 to 0.5). Pretest odds 0.61 x 0.4 = 0.24, and 0.24/(1 + 0.24) = 20%. The ratio is below 1, so the probability falls from 38%.
About 45% is the result for an intermediate impression (likelihood ratio 1.4). A low-probability impression has a ratio below 1, which lowers the probability below the 38% pretest value.
About 75% is the result for a HIGH probability impression (likelihood ratio 4.7). A ratio of 0.4 is below 1, so it decreases the probability rather than increasing it.
About 90% would require a likelihood ratio of about 15 and a rule-in result. A ratio of 0.4 is below 1, so it moves the probability down from 38%, not up.

questions.q:
A study was made of symptoms and physical findings in 247 patients evaluated for sinusitis. The final diagnosis was made according to x-ray findings (gold standard). Ninety-five patients had sinusitis, and 49 of them also had facial pain. One hundred fifty-two did not have sinusitis, and 79 of these patients had facial pain.

Given the answers for questions 4.7–4.9, which of the following statements is incorrect?
opts: A clinical impression of “high probability” of sinusitis is more useful in the management of patients than one of “low probability.”

This statement is true, so it is not the answer. About 75% probability of sinusitis makes treatment likely, whereas about 20% probability makes treatment unlikely, so a high-probability impression is the more decisive guide to management. Posttest probability informs treatment decisions.
A clinical impression of “intermediate probability” is approximately equivalent to a coin toss.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer. An intermediate impression gives roughly a 45% chance of sinusitis, which is close to 50-50, and its likelihood ratio (1.4) is indeterminate, so more investigation is usually needed.
Predictive value of facial pain will be higher in a clinical setting in which the prevalence of sinusitis is 10%.

Correct, because this is the false statement. Predictive values depend on prevalence: when disease is less common there are proportionally more false positives, so positive predictive value falls. At 10% prevalence, facial pain (sensitivity 52%, specificity 48%) would have a positive predictive value of only about 10%, lower than the 38% found here.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is most correct?
opts: Using diagnostic tests in parallel increases specificity and lowers positive predictive value.

Half of this is right: parallel testing does lower positive predictive value. But parallel testing generally INCREASES sensitivity and negative predictive value while it decreases specificity, since a positive on either test counts as positive.
Using diagnostic tests in series increases sensitivity and lowers positive predictive value.

This mixes up the two strategies. Serial testing (each later test done only after a positive result) maximizes specificity and positive predictive value and LOWERS sensitivity and negative predictive value, because a case missed by the first test is never retested.
Using diagnostic tests in parallel increases sensitivity and positive predictive value.

Parallel testing (all tests done at once) does raise sensitivity, so the disease is less likely to be missed, but it does not raise positive predictive value. It usually lowers specificity and positive predictive value because more people are flagged positive on at least one test.
Using diagnostic tests in series increases specificity and positive predictive value.

Correct. Serial testing requires a positive result on the earlier test before the next is done, which maximizes specificity and positive predictive value (fewer false positives), at the cost of lower sensitivity and negative predictive value.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is most correct?
opts: When using diagnostic tests in series, the test with the lowest sensitivity should be used first.

This reverses the rule of thumb. In serial testing the test with the HIGHEST specificity should generally go first, because it avoids unnecessary further testing in people without disease (unless another test is cheaper or less risky). Sensitivity is not the ordering criterion.
When using diagnostic tests in parallel or series, each test should contribute information independently.

Correct. Combining tests helps only if each one adds information that the others do not already provide. Parallel testing improves sensitivity only to the degree that the tests complement each other by detecting cases the other test misses, and the same idea applies in series.
When using diagnostic tests in parallel, the test with the highest specificity should be used first.

Parallel tests are conducted all at once, so there is no test to put first; the highest-specificity-first rule belongs to serial testing. Parallel testing is used when rapid diagnosis is preferred and mainly serves to raise sensitivity.

questions.q: In the mid-20th century, chest surgeons in Britain were impressed that they were operating on more men with lung cancer, most of whom were smoking. How might the surgeons' impression that smoking was a risk factor for developing lung cancer have been wrong?
opts: Smoking had become so common that more men would have a history of smoking, regardless of whether they were undergoing operations for lung cancer.

Correct. Smoking was common, so many men would be smokers whatever their illness. A high share of smokers among the patients does not by itself show increased risk without comparing how often smokers appear among people with and without lung cancer. A frequent exposure can be misread unless exposed and unexposed people are compared.
Lung cancer is an uncommon cancer, even among smokers.

Lung cancer is not an uncommon cancer; it is a common one. Even if it were rare, that would not explain why the surgeons' impression could be wrong. The flaw is the missing comparison group, not how often the cancer occurs.
Smoking confers a low risk of lung cancer.

Smoking is a strong risk factor for lung cancer, not a weak one, so this statement is false. The surgeons' impression could still be wrong because they never compared smoking rates in patients with and without the disease.
There are other risk factors for lung cancer.

Lung cancer does have other risk factors, but that does not make the impression about smoking wrong. A disease can have several risk factors, and the flaw here is that the surgeons made no comparison with people who did not have lung cancer.

questions.q: Risk factors are easier to recognize:
opts: When exposure to a risk factor occurs a long time before the disease.
A long time between exposure and disease (long latency) makes a risk harder to recognize, not easier, because the link between the exposure and the later illness is obscured by the passage of time.
When exposure to a risk factor is associated with a new disease

Correct. Risk factors are most readily recognized when an exposure is linked to a new disease, as happened with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). There are no established risk factors to compete with, and a large effect appearing soon after exposure is easy to recognize.
When the risk factor is a marker rather than a cause of disease.

Whether a factor is a marker or a cause does not decide how easily it is recognized. A marker predicts disease without causing it. Recognition depends on the size of the risk, how fast effects appear, latency, and how common the disease is.

questions.q: Risk prediction models are useful for:
opts: Predicting onset of disease

Predicting onset of disease is one legitimate use of risk prediction models, but it is not the only one. Because the models are also used to diagnose disease and to predict prognosis, selecting only this use is incomplete.
Diagnosing disease
Diagnosing disease is one use of risk prediction models, but not the only one. They are also used to predict onset of disease and to predict prognosis, so this single use is incomplete.
Predicting prognosis
Predicting prognosis (the course of disease once it is present) is one use of risk prediction models. They are also used to predict onset and to help diagnose, so choosing this alone is incomplete.
All of the above

Correct. Risk prediction models are used in all three situations: predicting onset of disease, diagnosing disease, and predicting prognosis. Each of the individual statements is true, so the combined option is the best answer.

questions.q: Figure 5.4C shows:
opts: The calibration is good, with predicted and observed rates the same.

Good calibration would put the points on or near the dotted diagonal line, where predicted and observed rates are equal. In this plot every point sits above that line, so predicted rates do not match observed rates.
The calibration is poor, with predicted rates consistently higher than observed rates.

Correct. Calibration compares the predicted probability with the observed proportion. Every point in the plot lies above the dotted line of perfect agreement, meaning the model predicted higher rates than actually occurred. In this plot the predicted probability is on the vertical axis and the observed proportion on the horizontal axis, so points above the line mean predicted rates are higher than observed. It consistently overestimates risk.
The calibration is poor, with predicted rates consistently lower than observed rates.
Predicted rates lower than observed would put the points below the dotted diagonal line. In this plot every point lies above it, so the model overestimates risk rather than underestimating it.
The calibration is poor, with predicted rates sometimes higher than observed rates, and other times lower than observed rates.

Mixed error would show points scattered on both sides of the dotted diagonal line. Here all the points fall on the same side, above it, so the error is consistently in one direction: predicted rates are always higher than observed.

questions.q: A risk model for colon cancer estimates that one of your patients has a 2% chance of developing colorectal cancer in the next 5 years. In explaining this to your patient, which of the following statements is most correct?
opts: Because colorectal cancer is the second most common nonskin cancer in men, he should be concerned about it.

A cancer being common in the population does not make this patient's own estimate high. Even for a common cancer there are groups with a low probability, and this patient's 2% over 5 years places him in a low-probability group.
The model shows that your patient will not develop colorectal cancer in the next 5 years.

A probability is not a certainty. A 2% chance means about 2 of every 100 similar people develop the cancer, so this patient is unlikely to, but he could be one of the few who do. The model cannot promise that he will not.
The model shows that your patient is a member of a group of people in whom a very small number will develop colorectal cancer in the next 5 years.

Correct. Risk estimates are probabilities based on groups. A 2% chance over 5 years means he belongs to a group in which very few people will develop colorectal cancer, though he could still be one of them.

questions.q: When a risk factor is a marker for future disease:
opts: The risk factor can help identify people at increased risk of developing the disease.

Correct. A marker is associated with future disease, so it helps identify people at increased risk, but it need not be a cause. That makes it useful for prediction but not necessarily a target for prevention.
Removing the risk factor can help prevent the disease.

Removing a marker does not prevent disease, because a marker is not a cause. Prevention by removing a risk factor works only when the factor is causal, such as controlling hypertension to prevent heart failure.
The risk factor is not confounding a true causal relationship.

A marker is usually tied to the disease through a confounder, an additional factor related to both the marker and the outcome. So the marker is typically confounded with the true cause rather than free of confounding.

questions.q: A risk factor is generally least useful in:
opts: The risk stratification process

Risk factors are useful in risk stratification, because risk estimates are probabilities based on groups sharing risk factors, which lets people be sorted by likelihood of future disease. This is a strength of risk factors, so it is not the answer.
Diagnosing a patient's complaint

Correct. Risk factors raise the probability of disease, but in an individual the best predictor of disease is the presence of early clinical disease itself. Symptoms, examination findings and tests matter more than risk factors when diagnosing a complaint.
Preventing disease

Prevention is a main use of risk factors: removing a causal risk factor lowers the probability of developing the disease, for example controlling hypertension to prevent heart failure. It is a strength, so it is not the answer.

questions.q: Figure 5.3B shows that:
opts: The risk model is well calibrated.

The figure shows how estimated risk is distributed in women who did and did not develop breast cancer. It does not compare predicted with observed rates, so it gives no direct information about calibration.
The risk model works well at stratifying women into different risk groups.

Stratifying would need the two groups to sit at different estimated risks. The two curves overlap almost completely, so the model does not separate women who developed breast cancer from those who did not.
Most women developing breast cancer over 5 years are at higher risk.

The curve for women who developed breast cancer is concentrated at low estimated risk and nearly reaches zero at the higher risks. Few of the women who developed breast cancer were at high risk, so this statement is false.
The risk model does not discriminate very well.

Correct. The curves for women who did and did not develop breast cancer almost overlap, with both peaking at low estimated risk. The model gives the two groups nearly the same estimates, so it discriminates poorly.

questions.q: It is difficult for risk models to determine which individuals will and will not develop disease for all of the following reasons except:
opts: The combination of risk factors is not strongly related to disease.

This is a genuine reason for difficulty. If the combination of risk factors is only weakly related to disease, it cannot separate people who will develop it from those who will not. Because the question asks for the exception, this is not the answer.
The risk factors are common throughout a population.

This is a genuine reason for difficulty. A risk factor present throughout a population cannot separate the people who will develop disease from those who will not. Because the question asks for the exception, this is not the answer.
The model is well calibrated.

Correct, this is the exception. Good calibration, meaning predicted rates match observed rates, does not impair discrimination. A model can be highly calibrated and still discriminate poorly, so calibration is not a reason for the difficulty.
Most people destined to develop the disease are not at high risk.

This is a genuine reason for difficulty. When most people who go on to develop the disease were not at high risk, high-risk labels miss most cases. Because the question asks for the exception, this is not the answer.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 5.9

questions.q: Which of the following is incorrect?
opts: Both diagnostic tests and prediction models can be assessed with sensitivity, specificity, and c-statistics.

This statement is correct, so it is not the answer. Diagnostic tests and prediction models can be assessed with similar methods, including sensitivity, specificity and the c-statistic, which summarizes discrimination.
Calibration is more important in prediction model assessment than diagnostic test evaluation.

This statement is correct, so it is not the answer. Calibration tends to be more important when assessing prediction models than when evaluating diagnostic tests, since a model's job is to give probabilities that match what happens.
Absolute risk estimates are usually a clinically relevant way to express risk.

This statement is correct, so it is not the answer. Absolute risk is the incidence of disease in a population, which tells a patient how likely disease is, and is usually a clinically relevant way to express risk.
A model with poor discrimination but excellent calibration cannot provide useful risk estimates.

Correct, this is the incorrect statement. A model with poor discrimination but excellent calibration can still provide useful risk estimates, because its predicted probabilities match observed rates even if it cannot separate individuals well.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 5.10

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not correct for both prospective and retrospective cohort studies?
opts: They measure incidence of disease directly.

That is true of both designs, so it is not the exception: because the cohort is followed forward from exposure (or reconstructed from records with known follow-up), new cases are counted directly, which is why cohort studies, unlike case-control studies, establish incidence directly.
They allow assessment of possible associations between exposure and many diseases.

That is true of both designs, so it is not the exception: a cohort is defined by its exposure, and once followed it can be checked for many different outcomes, so the relationship between one exposure and a number of diseases can be assessed.
They allow investigators to decide beforehand what data to collect.

Correct, this is the statement that is NOT true of both. Only a prospective cohort lets investigators decide beforehand what to collect; a retrospective (historical) cohort must use records made earlier for other purposes, so it cannot examine characteristics that were never recorded and exposure may not have been measured in a standardized way.
They avoid bias that might occur if measurement of exposure is made after the outcome of interest is known.

That is true of both designs, so it is not the exception: exposure is documented without knowledge of the outcome (in a historical cohort, the exposure was recorded before the outcome occurred), which avoids the recall bias that afflicts case-control studies, where exposure is asked about after disease is known.

questions.q:
A study was done examining the relationship of smoking, stroke, and age. The 12-year incidence per 1,000 persons (absolute risk) of stroke according to age and smoking status was:

45–49: Nonsmokers 7.4, Smokers 29.7; 65–69: Nonsmokers 80.2, Smokers 110.4.

What was the relative risk of stroke of smokers compared to nonsmokers in their 40s?
opts: That is the relative risk for the 65-69 age group (110.4 divided by 80.2 = 1.4), not the 40s group the question asks about; relative risk must be calculated with the incidences from the correct age stratum.

Correct: relative risk is the incidence in exposed persons divided by the incidence in non-exposed persons, so for the 40s it is 29.7 / 7.4 = 4.0, meaning smokers in their 40s were about 4 times as likely to have a stroke.
That is the attributable risk in the 40s (29.7 minus 7.4 = 22.3 per 1,000), a difference of incidences; relative risk is a ratio of them (29.7 divided by 7.4), not a difference.
That is the attributable risk in the 60s (110.4 minus 80.2 = 30.2 per 1,000), a difference rather than a ratio and from the wrong age group; relative risk for the 40s is the ratio 29.7 / 7.4.

That number (80.2 minus 7.4 = 72.8) subtracts the nonsmoker incidence in one age group from the nonsmoker incidence in the other; it compares age groups, not smokers with nonsmokers, and it is a difference, not a ratio.

That number (110.4 minus 29.7 = 80.7) subtracts the smoker incidence in the 40s from the smoker incidence in the 60s; it compares age groups, not smokers with nonsmokers, and it is a difference rather than the ratio 29.7 / 7.4 = 4.0.

What was the attributable risk per 1,000 people of stroke among smokers compared to nonsmokers in their 60s?

That number (80.2 minus 7.4 = 72.8) subtracts the nonsmoker incidence in the 40s from the nonsmoker incidence in the 60s; it compares age groups rather than smokers with nonsmokers, so it is not attributable to smoking.

questions.q:
A study was done examining the relationship of smoking, stroke, and age. The 12-year incidence per 1,000 persons (absolute risk) of stroke according to age and smoking status was:

45–49: Nonsmokers 7.4, Smokers 29.7; 65–69: Nonsmokers 80.2, Smokers 110.4.

Which of the following statements about the study results is incorrect?
opts: To calculate population-attributable risk of smoking among people in their 60s, additional data are needed.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: population attributable risk depends on how common the risk factor is in the whole population (how many people are exposed), and the prevalence of smoking in people in their 60s is not given, so more data are needed.
More cases of stroke due to smoking occurred in people in their 60s than in their 40s.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: the extra strokes attributable to smoking were 110.4 minus 80.2 = 30.2 per 1,000 in the 60s versus 29.7 minus 7.4 = 22.3 per 1,000 in the 40s, so more strokes were due to smoking in the older group even though its relative risk was lower.
When relative risk is calculated, the results reflect information about the incidence in exposed and unexposed persons, whereas the results for attributable risk do not.

Correct, this statement is the incorrect one. Both measures are built from the incidence in exposed and in unexposed persons: relative risk is their ratio and attributable risk is their difference. What differs is that the ratio hides how large the absolute incidence is, but it still uses both incidences.
The calculated relative risk is a stronger argument for smoking as cause of stroke for persons in their 40s than the calculated risk for persons in their 60s.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: the relative risk is 4.0 in the 40s but only 1.4 in the 60s, and a stronger association is better evidence for a causal role than a weaker one, even though the absolute excess is larger in the 60s.
Depending on the question asked, age could be considered as either a confounding variable or an effect modifier in the study.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: because the effect of smoking differs by age (relative risk 4.0 versus 1.4), age acts as an effect modifier, which is not a bias; if age were instead related to both smoking and stroke and distorted the association, it would be handled as a confounder.

questions.q:
Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is a serious condition that occasionally can lead to pulmonary embolism and death. The incidence of DVT is increased by several genetic and environmental factors, including oral contraceptives (OCs) and a genetic mutation, factor V Leiden. These two risk factors, OCs and factor V Leiden, interact. Heterozygotes for factor V Leiden have 4 to 10 times the risk of DVT of the general population. In women without the genetic mutation, incidence of DVT rises from about 0.8/10,000 women/yr among those not on OCs to 3.0/10,000 women/yr for those taking the pill. The baseline incidence of DVT in heterozygotes for factor V Leiden is 5.7/10,000 women/yr, rising to 28.5/10,000 women/yr among those taking OCs. Mutations for factor V Leiden occur in about 5% of whites but are absent in Africans and Asians.

What is the absolute risk of DVT in women who do not have the mutation and do not take OCs?
opts: Correct: absolute risk is another term for incidence, the number of new cases over a period divided by the people in the group, and in women with neither the mutation nor oral contraceptive use it is 0.8 per 10,000 women per year.

That is the population attributable risk from 25.5 per 10,000 times a prevalence of 0.05 (25.5 x 0.05 = 1.3); it applies to a population of oral contraceptive users, not to the baseline group, whose absolute risk is the plain incidence.
That is the attributable risk of oral contraceptives in women without the mutation (3.0 minus 0.8 = 2.2), a difference; absolute risk for the baseline group is just its incidence, 0.8.

That is the relative risk in women on oral contraceptives (28.5 divided by 3.0 = 9.5), a unitless ratio; absolute risk is an incidence in cases per 10,000 women per year and needs no comparison group.
That is the attributable risk of the mutation in oral contraceptive users (28.5 minus 3.0 = 25.5), a difference between two groups; the baseline group's absolute risk is simply its own incidence.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 17; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 6.5

That is the attributable risk of the mutation among oral contraceptive users (28.5 minus 3.0); the question is about the excess from taking oral contraceptives in women without the mutation, which is 3.0 minus 0.8.

That is the attributable risk for a carrier (28.5 minus 3.0 = 25.5), which applies only to women who have the mutation; multiplying by the 5% prevalence spreads that excess across the whole population and gives 1.3.

The incidence of DVT is increased by several genetic and environmental factors, including oral contraceptives (OCs) and a genetic mutation, factor V Leiden. These two risk factors, OCs and factor V Leiden, interact. Heterozygotes for factor V Leiden have 4 to 10 times the risk of DVT of the general population. In women without the genetic mutation, incidence of DVT rises from about 0.8/10,000 women/yr among those not on OCs to 3.0/10,000 women/yr for those taking the pill. Mutations for factor V Leiden occur in about 5% of whites but are absent in Africans and Asians.

Given the information in this study and calculations for questions 6.5– 6.10, which of the following statements about risk of developing DVT is incorrect?
opts: Women heterozygous for factor V Leiden should be advised against taking OCs because of the high relative risk for DVT among such women.

Correct, this is the incorrect statement, because its reasoning rests on relative risk alone. The relative risk is high (28.5 / 5.7 = 5.0 compared with carriers who do not take oral contraceptives), but the absolute risk stays small (about 5.7 rising to 28.5 per 10,000 per year), and absolute or attributable risk shows the real clinical consequence. Counseling should give the patient those absolute numbers along with her other risk factors, not the relative risk alone.
Factor V Leiden modifies the effect of OCs on the annual risk of developing DVT by increasing risk from about 3 per 10,000 to about 30 per 10,000 women.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: the presence of the mutation changes the effect of oral contraceptives, taking the risk among users from 3.0 per 10,000 (non-carriers) to 28.5 per 10,000 (carriers), about 30. A variable that changes the effect of an exposure is an effect modifier, and it is not a bias.
Being heterozygous for factor V Leiden confers about twice the risk for DVT as taking OCs.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: the mutation alone gives a relative risk of 5.7 / 0.8 = 7.1 while oral contraceptives alone give 3.0 / 0.8 = 3.8, so the mutation carries about 7.1 / 3.8 = 1.9 times, roughly twice, the risk.

questions.q: In a study to determine if regularly taking aspirin prevents cardiovascular death, aspirin users died as often as nonusers. However, aspirin users were sicker and had illnesses more likely to be treated with aspirin. Which of the following methods is the best way to account for the propensity of people to take aspirin?
opts: Calculate the absolute risk of cardiovascular death in the two groups and the risk difference attributable to using aspirin.

This does not remove the problem: absolute risk and the risk difference are just incidence and attributable risk from the crude comparison, so they still mix in the fact that sicker people chose aspirin; describing risk is not a way of controlling confounding.
Create subgroups of aspirin users and nonusers with similar indications for using the medication and compare death rates among the subgroups.

Correct: the degree of illness that led to aspirin use is a confounder, related both to taking aspirin and to dying. Stratification compares death rates within subgroups of users and non-users who have otherwise similar indications, so illness severity is held constant within each stratum.
For each person using aspirin, match a nonuser on age, sex, and comorbidity and compare death rates in the two groups.

Matching is a valid way to control confounding, but only for the characteristics that were matched. Age, sex and comorbidity may not capture the specific indications that led sicker people to take aspirin, so some confounding by indication can remain, whereas comparing users with nonusers within subgroups of similar indication addresses that confounder directly.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: In a case-control study of oral contraceptives and myocardial infarction (heart attack), exposure to birth control pills was abstracted from medical records at the time of the myocardial infarction. Results might be biased toward finding an association by all of the following except:
opts: Physicians might have asked about use of birth control pill more carefully in cases.

This could bias the study toward an association: if physicians questioned cases more carefully about pill use, exposure would be found more often in cases than in controls, which inflates the odds ratio.
Having a myocardial infarction might have led to oral contraceptive use.

Correct. This is the exception. Pill use abstracted from records at the time of the infarction reflects use that came before the event, so the infarction cannot have led to it and creates no false excess of exposure in cases. The other statements each describe exposure being asked about, recorded, abstracted, or recalled more readily in cases, which falsely raises the odds ratio.
Physicians might have been more likely to record birth control use in cases.
This could bias the study toward an association: if physicians recorded pill use more often for cases, exposure looks more frequent in cases than it truly was, which falsely raises the odds ratio.
Medical record abstractors might have looked for evidence of oral contraceptive use more carefully if they knew a patient had had a myocardial infarction.

This could bias the study toward an association: abstractors who know a patient had a myocardial infarction may search harder for pill use, so exposure is found more often in cases and the odds ratio is falsely elevated.
Patients might have recalled exposure more readily when they had a heart attack.

This is recall bias: subjects asked about past exposure may remember it better once they have the disease being studied, so cases report exposure more readily than controls and the association is exaggerated.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: Investigators in Europe did a case-control study, nested in a multicountry cohort of more than 520,000 participants, of vitamin D concentration and the risk of colon cancer. They studied 1,248 cases of incident colon cancer arising in the cohort and an equal number of controls, sampled from the same cohort and matched by age, sex, and study center. Vitamin D was measured in blood samples taken years before diagnosis. Vitamin D levels were lower in patients with colon cancer, independent of a rich array of potentially confounding variables. The study results could be described by any of the following except:
opts: Vitamin D deficiency was a cause of colorectal cancer.

Correct. A case-control study, even a well-designed one nested in a cohort, cannot claim to have identified a cause: unmeasured confounding is always possible, and risk factors may predict disease without causing it (they may be disease markers).
Vitamin D levels were associated with colorectal cancer.

This can be said: lower vitamin D levels were found more often in patients with colon cancer, and an association is exactly what a case-control comparison of exposure between cases and controls measures.
Vitamin D deficiency was a risk factor for colorectal cancer.

This can be said: vitamin D was measured years before diagnosis, so the low level came before the cancer, and a factor linked to a higher probability of developing disease later fits the definition of a risk factor.
Nesting the study in a large cohort was a strength of the study.

This can be said: sampling controls from the same large cohort as the cases gives a source population that is clearly defined, and exposure was measured in stored blood before diagnosis rather than recalled, which is a strength.
The results might have been confounded with unmeasured variables related to vitamin D levels and colorectal cancer.

This can be said: adjusting for measured confounders cannot remove the effect of confounders that were never measured, so the results might still be confounded by unmeasured variables related to both vitamin D and cancer.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: Which of the following is the most direct result of a case-control study?
opts: Prevalence

Prevalence is the portion of a group with a condition at one point in time, usually found from a survey or cross-sectional study; a case-control study starts from chosen cases and controls, so it cannot give it.
Odds ratio

Correct. The odds ratio (relative odds) is the measure of association for case-control studies, calculated as the odds of exposure in cases divided by the odds of exposure in controls, which equals ad over bc; it serves as an estimated relative risk.
Risk difference

A risk difference (attributable risk) is the incidence in exposed persons minus the incidence in unexposed persons, so it needs incidence, which a case-control study cannot supply because the numbers of cases and controls are chosen by the investigator.
Relative risk

Relative risk is the ratio of incidence in exposed to incidence in unexposed persons and is the measure for cohort studies; a case-control study yields the odds ratio instead, which only estimates relative risk.
Incidence

Incidence, the number of new cases over a given time in a group, is established directly by cohort studies; a case-control study begins with cases and controls already selected, so it cannot report incidence.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: The epidemic curve for an acute infectious disease describes:
opts: The usual incubation period for the causal agent

The usual incubation period is a property of the organism, not what an epidemic curve shows; the curve plots cases against time of onset, and only its shape may hint at the interval between exposure and illness.
A comparison of illness over time in exposed versus nonexposed people
An epidemic curve does not compare exposed with nonexposed people; that comparison is made with attack rates or a cohort or case-control analysis. The curve plots only the number of cases over time.
The onset of illness in cases over time

Correct. An epidemic (epi) curve is the number of cases plotted against time, usually by date of onset of illness, so it shows the rise and fall of cases over the course of the outbreak, as in the Legionnaires' disease outbreak plotted by date of onset.
The duration of illness, on average, in affected individuals
The curve marks when illness began in each case, not how long each person stayed ill, so it does not give the average duration of illness; duration would need recovery dates.
The distribution of time from infection to first symptoms
The distribution of time from infection to first symptoms is the incubation period distribution; an epidemic curve counts cases by onset date and does not record each person's time of infection.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: Which of the following is the best reason for doing a case-control analysis of a cohort study?
opts: Case-control studies are a feasible way of controlling for confounders not found in the cohort dataset.

Correct. If the cohort data lack variables that should be controlled for, a case-control analysis within the cohort is more efficient because the extra data need to be collected only for the cases and a sample of controls, not for the entire cohort.
Case-control studies can provide all the same information more easily.
A case-control study cannot provide all the same information: it gives an odds ratio (an estimate of relative risk) but cannot establish incidence, which a cohort study measures directly.
Case-control studies can determine incidence of disease in exposed and nonexposed members of the cohort.

Incidence in exposed and nonexposed members is calculated directly from the whole cohort; a case-control study, which samples cases and controls, cannot determine incidence, so it is not the reason for this analysis.
Case-control studies are in general stronger than cohort studies.

Case-control studies are not in general stronger than cohort studies; they are a step earlier in the usual study sequence and are limited by recall bias and dependence on choosing controls. Their advantage here is efficiency.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: The best way to identify cases is to obtain them from:
opts: A sample from the general (dynamic) population

A sample from a dynamic population is less good because exposure or disease may be changing over time, and controls may not be matched to the date each case developed disease. A defined cohort avoids these problems.
Primary care physicians' offices

Primary care offices capture only people who present there, who may differ from the population that produced the cases, which invites selection bias; sampling from a cohort gives cases from a clearly defined source.
A community
A community is a looser source than a cohort: the group is not clearly defined and followed, so it is harder to be sure cases and controls come from the same source population.
A cohort representative of the population

Correct. Sampling cases (and controls) from a cohort representative of the population is best, especially when exposure or disease changes rapidly over time or when controls are not matched to the date of disease onset in cases.
A hospital

Hospital patients are a convenient source but may differ systematically from everyone who has the disease, which can create selection bias; a cohort representative of the population is the better source.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.6

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: What is the best reason to include multiple control groups in a case-control study?
opts: To obtain a stronger estimate of relative risk
Multiple control groups do not strengthen the estimate of relative risk; they test whether the odds ratio is robust, or sensitive, to the type of control group chosen.
There are a limited number of cases and an ample number of potential controls
Having few cases and many potential controls is the reason to use several controls per case, which adds statistical power. That is different from using multiple control groups of different types.
To control for confounding
Confounding is controlled by matching, stratification, or adjustment; adding another control group does not remove a confounder, though it may reveal that the results depend on the controls chosen.
To increase the generalizability of the result
Generalizability depends on how representative the sampled cases and controls are of the wider population; adding control groups does not by itself broaden that.
The main control group may be systematically different from cases (other than on the exposure of interest)

Correct. The main control group may differ from the cases in ways other than the exposure of interest; using a second control group shows whether results change substantially, and if they do the findings are called into question.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.7

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: A case-control study was conducted based on a registry of 10,000 children that were genetically predisposed to develop celiac disease (characterized by sensitivity to gluten in the diet that can lead to malabsorption). Investigators wanted to see if enterovirus infection was associated with increased risk of developing the disease in these children. The children were followed with regular blood and stool tests for 10 years. After 10 years, a sample of 100 cases was selected from 2,000 children who developed the disease, and 20% of these children had a preceding enterovirus infection. 200 Controls were selected from the remaining children without the disease, and 13% of these children had enterovirus diagnosed. Which of the following is true?
opts: They crude odds ratio provides a good approximation of crude relative risk.

Not here: the odds ratio approximates relative risk well only when the disease is rare, and in this registry 2,000 of 10,000 children (20%) developed celiac disease, which is common. The crude odds ratio is about 1.67, from (0.20 / 0.80) divided by (0.13 / 0.87).
The sampling method for controls is inappropriate because only noncases are studied.

Controls in every case-control study come from noncases, because the control group is defined as people without the condition, so that alone is not a flaw. The problem is when they are sampled and how frequent the disease is.
The crude odds ratio will overestimate relative risk.

Correct. Controls were chosen from children still disease-free after the study ended, and the disease is common (20%), so the odds ratio overestimates relative risk when it is above 1. Here the crude odds ratio is about 1.67, while a relative risk worked out for the whole registry (assuming the sampled exposure percentages hold for all cases and noncases) is about 1.5.
The control selection will provide a direct estimate of population exposure.

Controls drawn only from children who stayed disease-free do not represent the exposure of the whole registry, which includes the 20% who developed disease; population-based sampling of noncases throughout the study would be needed for that.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 36; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 5; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.8

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: Case-control studies can be used to study all of the following except:
opts: The early symptoms of stomach cancer
A case-control study can do this: it compares people with stomach cancer with people without it, looking back at symptoms and other features that came earlier in the cases.
Risk factors for sudden infant death syndrome

A case-control study can do this: sudden infant death syndrome is rare, and case-control studies are better than cohorts for rare disease because they need small samples and no waiting for the condition to develop.
The incidence of suicide in the adult population

Correct. Incidence is the number of new cases over time in a population of known size; case-control studies choose their cases and controls, so they cannot provide incidence (a cohort study establishes incidence directly).
The protective effect of aspirin
A case-control study can do this: if aspirin protects, it will be less common among cases than controls, giving an odds ratio below 1, which indicates a possible protective association.
Modes of transmission of an infectious disease
A case-control study can do this: comparing infected people with uninfected people for exposures such as foods or contacts shows how the disease is being spread, which is a common use in outbreaks.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: In a case-control study of exercise and sudden cardiac death, matching would be useful:
opts: To control for all potential confounding variables in the study
Matching controls only the few variables that are matched. Other confounders, including unmeasured ones, are handled by other methods such as stratification or adjustment in the analysis.
To make cases and controls similar to each other with respect to a few major characteristics

Correct. Matching selects controls with the same characteristics as cases on a few major variables (for example age and sex) except the exposure under study, so cases and controls do not differ on those variables that might be strongly related to exposure or disease.
To make it possible to examine the effects of the matched variables on estimated relative risk

Matching makes cases and controls equal on the matched variables, so it removes the differences needed to study their effects; the effect of a matched variable on the estimated relative risk cannot be examined.
To test whether the right controls were chosen for the cases in the study
Testing whether the right controls were chosen is the job of a second, different control group; matching does not test control selection but builds similarity into it.
To increase the generalizability of the study

Matching does not improve generalizability; it forces controls to resemble the cases, which if anything ties the comparison to that type of person rather than broadening the population the results apply to.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 27; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.10

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: In a case-control study of whether prolonged air travel is a risk factor for venous thromboembolism, 60 out of 100 cases and 40 out of 100 controls had prolonged air travel. What was the crude odds ratio from this study?
opts: 0.44 is the reciprocal of the correct value (40 x 40 divided by 60 x 60): the cases' exposure odds were put on the bottom instead of the top. That would make the exposure look protective when it was more common in cases.

1.5 is only the odds of air travel in cases (60/40, or the ratio of 60% to 40%); it ignores the controls. The odds ratio divides the case odds (1.5) by the control odds (40/60, about 0.67), giving 2.25.
Correct. Odds of air travel in cases = 60/40 = 1.5; odds in controls = 40/60 = 0.67; odds ratio = 1.5 / 0.67 = 2.25, the same as the cross products (60 x 60) / (40 x 40) = 3,600 / 1,600.
No valid arrangement of these counts produces 3.0; the cross-product ratio of the 2 x 2 table (60 exposed and 40 unexposed cases; 40 exposed and 60 unexposed controls) is 3,600 / 1,600 = 2.25.
Not possible to calculate
The odds ratio can be calculated: the numbers of exposed and unexposed cases (60 and 40) and controls (40 and 60) fill every cell of the 2 x 2 table, and that is all the odds ratio requires.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 38; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 36; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.11

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: A population-based case-control study would be especially useful for studying:
opts: The population attributable risk of disease
Population attributable risk depends on the incidence of disease in the population, and case-control studies cannot supply incidence because cases and controls are selected by the investigator.
Multiple outcomes (diseases)
A case-control study begins with one outcome (disease or no disease) and looks back at exposures. Studying multiple outcomes is an advantage of cohort studies, which follow an exposure forward.
The incidence of rare diseases

Case-control studies are well suited to rare disease, but they cannot report incidence, since the number of cases and controls is set by the investigator; incidence is established directly by cohort studies.
The prevalence of disease
Prevalence, the portion of a group with a condition at a point in time, comes from cross-sectional (prevalence) studies of a population, not from a case-control study.
Risk factors for disease

Correct. A case-control study compares people with and without one disease for earlier exposure, so it is useful for identifying risk factors for that disease, giving an odds ratio that estimates relative risk.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 35; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 14; 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.12

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: The prevalence odds ratio of rheumatoid arthritis provides an estimate of:
opts: The relative risk of arthritis
Relative risk requires incidence (new cases) in exposed and unexposed groups. An odds ratio from prevalent cases mixes new and long-standing cases, so it is not a comparison of risk.
The attributable risk of arthritis
Attributable risk is the incidence in exposed persons minus the incidence in unexposed persons; a prevalence odds ratio uses existing cases, not incidence, so it cannot estimate it.
Risk factors for the duration of arthritis

A prevalence odds ratio cannot isolate risk factors for how long the disease lasts. Prevalent cases include people who developed disease long ago and are still affected, so a characteristic could relate to duration or onset, and the two cannot be separated.
The association between a patient characteristic and prevalence of arthritis

Correct. An odds ratio based on prevalent cases gives a rough measure of the association between a patient characteristic and having arthritis at that point in time, but not a comparison of risk, which requires incident (new-onset) cases.
Risk factors for the incidence of arthritis

Risk factors for the incidence of arthritis would need newly developing (incident) cases. Prevalent cases include people who developed arthritis earlier, so this odds ratio cannot show what raises the risk of new disease.

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: A case-control study was conducted to determine if children with asthma who used inhaled corticosteroids are at increased risk of fractures. A national registry was used to select cases and population-based controls, and possible confounders assessed by phone interview and chart review. Which of the following is incorrect?
opts: Matching on sex would remove confounding for this factor
This statement is correct, so it is not the answer: matching controls to cases on sex makes the two groups alike on sex, which removes confounding by that factor.
If there is no difference between the crude and adjusted odds ratio, then confounding for the measured factors was not present

This statement is correct: a confounder is related to both exposure and outcome, so if adjusting for a measured factor leaves the odds ratio unchanged from the crude value, that factor was not confounding the result.
Incidence of fracture in children using corticosteroids cannot be estimated

This statement is correct: case-control studies select cases and controls and give odds ratios, so the incidence of fracture in steroid users cannot be estimated (a cohort study establishes incidence directly).
This study can identify risk factors but not establish cause

This statement is correct: an association found in a case-control study can identify a risk factor and support an argument for causation, but risk factors may predict disease without being a cause, so it cannot establish cause alone.
Difference in rates of participation in recreational sports between cases and controls would show that control selection was biased

Correct. This is the incorrect statement. A difference in sports participation between cases and controls may be a real association (sports may raise fracture risk) or a confounder, and does not prove that control selection was biased.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 27; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 6; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.14

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: In an outbreak of acute gastroenteritis, a case-control study would be especially useful for identifying:
opts: Characteristics of the people affected

Describing who was affected (age, sex, and so on) is done by characterizing cases by time, place, and person during the outbreak investigation; it needs only a description of the cases, not a comparison with controls.
The number of people affected over time
The number of people affected over time is shown by the epidemic curve, which plots cases against time (by onset), and needs only the cases; no comparison with controls is required.
The microbe or toxin causing the outbreak
The microbe or toxin is usually known early or found by establishing the diagnosis, with laboratory testing of cases; a case-control comparison of exposures does not identify the organism.
The mode of transmission

Correct. Comparing the exposures of ill and well people tests hypotheses about how the disease is being spread (mode of transmission). That is the most pressing question, and answering it allows the outbreak to be controlled and its source traced.
Where the causative agent originated
The original source is traced after hypotheses have been tested, using what is found about how the disease is spread; the case-control comparison itself mainly identifies the route or vehicle.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 38; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 39; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.15

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: Sampling cases and controls from a defined population or cohort accomplishes which of the following?
opts: It tends to include cases and controls that are representative of the source population.

Correct. Taking all or a random sample of cases and a random sample of controls from a defined population or cohort gives cases and controls that resemble those in the source population, reducing selection bias.
It is the only way of including incident (new) cases of disease.
It is not the only way of including incident cases; new-onset cases can be found by other means. Sampling from a defined group simply makes the cases and controls more representative of it.
It avoids the need for inclusion and exclusion criteria.
It does not avoid the need for inclusion and exclusion criteria; cases and controls must still meet the same definitions of who qualifies, or the groups will differ for reasons other than exposure.
It matches cases and controls on important variables.
Sampling from a population does not match cases and controls; matching is a separate design step that picks controls with the same characteristics as cases on selected variables.
It ensures that the results are generalizable.
It does not ensure generalizability; the results apply to people like the source population, and study patients may not represent other populations or individual patients.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.16

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: Case-control studies would be useful for answering all of the following questions except:
opts: Do cholesterol-lowering drugs prevent coronary heart disease?

A case-control study can be useful here: it can compare cholesterol-lowering drug use in people with and without coronary heart disease, and a protective effect appears as an odds ratio below 1 (a randomized trial is stronger evidence, but this study type can address the question).
Are complications more common with fiberoptic cholecystectomy than with conventional (open) surgery?

A case-control study can be useful here: comparing patients with and without a complication for the type of surgery received gives an odds ratio that shows whether complications were associated with the fiberoptic approach.
Is drinking alcohol a risk factor for breast cancer?
A case-control study is well suited to this: comparing alcohol use in women with and without breast cancer identifies risk factors, and an odds ratio above 1 indicates a risk factor.
How often do complications occur after fiberoptic cholecystectomy?

Correct. How often complications occur is an incidence question, and case-control studies do not provide incidence because the numbers of cases and controls are selected by the investigator; a cohort study is needed.
How effective are antibiotics for otitis media?

A case-control study can address this: comparing antibiotic treatment in children with and without treatment failure gives an odds ratio, though the strongest evidence for effectiveness comes from a randomized trial.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 14; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 35; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.17

questions.io: Chapter 7 · Risk: From Disease to Exposure
questions.q: In a case-control study of airplane flight and thrombophlebitis, all of the following conditions should be met for the odds ratio to be a reasonable estimate of relative risk except:
opts: Controls were sampled from the same population as cases.

This condition should be met: controls must come from the same population as the cases, because otherwise the two groups differ for reasons other than exposure, and the odds ratio would not estimate the relative risk in that population.
Cases and controls met the same inclusion and exclusion criteria.
This condition should be met: cases and controls must meet the same inclusion and exclusion criteria, or differences between the groups other than the exposure will distort the odds ratio.
Other variables that might be related to air travel and thrombosis were controlled for.

This condition should be met: confounders related to both air travel and thrombosis must be controlled by matching, stratification, or adjustment, or they bias the odds ratio away from the true relative risk.
Cases and controls were equally susceptible to developing thrombophlebitis (e.g., were equally mobile, weight, recent trauma, previous VTE) other than for air travel.

This condition should be met: if cases and controls differed in susceptibility (immobility, weight, trauma, previous venous thromboembolism) apart from air travel, the comparison would be biased, so they must be equally susceptible.
The incidence of thrombophlebitis was more than 5/100.

Correct. This is the exception: the odds ratio approximates relative risk when the disease is rare (a rule of thumb is under about 1 in 100 to 5 in 100), so high incidence is not a requirement. When the disease is more common and controls are sampled from noncases after the study, the odds ratio overestimates relative risk when it is above 1.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 36; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 5; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 7.18

questions.q: For a study of the risk of esophageal cancer in patients with Barrett esophagus (a precancerous lesion), which of the following times in the course of disease is the best example of zero time?
opts: Diagnosis of Barrett esophagus for each patient

Correct. Zero time is the point in the disease course at which every member of an inception cohort is assembled, ideally as early and as uniformly as possible. Here that is the diagnosis of Barrett esophagus, the condition that defines the cohort, and esophageal cancer is the outcome being followed.
Death of each patient

Death is an endpoint of follow-up, not the starting point. Zero time is when patients are identified at a similar point in the disease course, so death cannot serve as the time at which the cohort is assembled.
Diagnosis of esophageal cancer for each patient

Esophageal cancer is the outcome this study is measuring, so its diagnosis marks an event during follow-up. Zero time must come at the onset of the condition that defines the cohort (Barrett esophagus), not at the outcome.
Calendar time when the first patient is enrolled in the study

Patients are enrolled on different calendar dates, and zero time is defined by where each patient is in the course of disease rather than by the calendar. Following everyone from the same point in disease, such as diagnosis, is what makes the cohort comparable.
Calendar time when no patient remains in the study
The calendar time when no patient remains marks the end of the study, not its beginning. Zero time is the common starting point in the disease course from which each patient's follow-up is counted.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 8; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.1

questions.q: A cohort study describes the recurrence of seizure within 1 year in children hospitalized with a first febrile seizure. It compared recurrence in children who had infection versus immunization as an underlying cause for fever at the time of the first seizure. Some of the children were no longer in the study when outcome (a second seizure) was assessed at 1 year. Which of the following would have the greatest effect on study results?
opts: Why the children dropped out

The reason matters only through its link to prognosis. Dropouts distort results when they differ in prognosis from those who stay (for example, leaving because of recovery or worsening), so the deciding question is whether leaving was related to prognosis, not the stated reason alone.
When in the course of follow-up the children left the study

The timing of leaving can change how much follow-up each child contributes, but it does not by itself distort the comparison. What matters most is whether the children who left had a different prognosis from those who stayed.
Whether dropping out was related to prognosis

Correct. Migration bias arises when patients drop out and those who leave are not similar to those who stay. Dropping out distorts the results only if it is related to prognosis, for example if children who were more likely to have a second seizure left; as the proportion of dropouts grows, so does the potential for bias.
Whether the number of children dropping out is similar in the groups

Similar numbers of dropouts in the two groups do not protect the results. If the children who left one group had a different prognosis from those who left the other, the comparison is still biased; what counts is whether leaving was related to prognosis.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 23; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.2

questions.q: A cohort study of prostate cancer care compares rates of incontinence in patients who were treated with surgery versus medical care alone. Incontinence is assessed from review of medical records. Which of the following is not an example of measurement bias?
opts: Men were more likely to tell their surgeon about incontinence.

This is a form of measurement bias. If men who had surgery were more likely to report incontinence to their surgeon, the outcome was more likely to be detected in that group than in the medical care group.
Surgeons were less likely to record complications of their surgery in the record.

This is a form of measurement bias. If complications of surgery were recorded less often, incontinence was less likely to be detected in the surgery group, so the two groups were not measured equally.
Men who got surgery were more likely to have follow-up visits.

This is a form of measurement bias. More follow-up visits give the surgery group more chances to have incontinence noted, which raises the likelihood that the outcome is detected there compared with the other group.
Chart abstractors used their judgment is deciding whether incontinence was present or not.
This is a form of measurement bias. When abstractors rely on their own judgment, the outcome is classified by inconsistent methods; strict criteria and blinding are how measurement bias is minimized.
Rates of incontinence were higher in the men who got surgery.

Correct. A higher rate of incontinence in men who had surgery is the study result, and it can reflect a true effect of surgery. Measurement bias means one group is more likely to have its outcome detected or classified differently, so a difference in rates is not itself a measurement error.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 24; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.3

questions.q: A clinical prediction rule has been developed to classify the prognosis of community-acquired pneumonia. Which of the following is most characteristic of such a clinical prediction rule?
opts: Calculating a score is simple.

This is a genuine feature, but not the whole answer. Simple score calculation is indeed a feature of clinical prediction rules, but it is not the only one; being simple, using available data, including several factors and guiding management all characterize these rules, so all of them apply.
The clinical data are readily available.

This is a genuine feature, but not the whole answer. Readily available clinical data is a feature of prediction rules, but so are simple calculation, multiple prognostic factors and guiding management, which makes all of them apply.
Multiple prognostic factors are included.

This is a genuine feature, but not the whole answer. A rule combines multiple prognostic factors, because several factors predict outcome better than a single data point, but it also uses simple scoring and available data and guides management.
The results are used to guide further management of the patient.

This is a genuine feature, but not the whole answer. Results of the rule are used to guide further management, but this is one of four features, and the rule is also simple to score, uses readily available data and includes multiple factors.
All of the above.

Correct. A clinical prediction rule estimates the probability of an outcome from a set of patient characteristics (multiple prognostic factors, which predict better than any single data point), and such rules are also simple to score, use readily available clinical data and guide further management.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.4

questions.q: A study describes the clinical course of patients who have an uncommon neurologic disease. Patients are identified at a referral center that specializes in this disease. Their medical records are reviewed for patients' characteristics, treatments, and their current disease status. Which of the following best describes this kind of study?
opts: Cohort study

A cohort study assembles a group at a similar point in the disease course and follows it over time to measure outcomes. Here patients were simply identified at a referral center and their records reviewed for characteristics, treatments and current status, which is descriptive rather than a defined follow-up of a cohort.
Case-control study

A case-control study defines groups by outcome (disease or no disease) and compares exposures between them. This study has no comparison group without the disease; it only describes a group of patients who have it.
Case series

Correct. A case series is a descriptive design that reports the characteristics of a group of patients, here those seen at a referral center with an uncommon disease, without an inception cohort, a comparison group or a representative sample. It gives a description of the clinical course, not relative risk.
Cross-sectional study

A cross-sectional (prevalence) study assesses a population for a condition at a single point in time. This study describes patients drawn from a specialty referral center, not a representative sample of everyone with the disease, and it reports treatments and clinical course.
A randomized controlled trial
A randomized controlled trial is experimental, meaning the investigator assigns the intervention. In this study treatments were only recorded from medical records, so nothing was assigned.
questions.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8; 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 10; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.5

questions.q: A study used time-to-event analysis to describe the survival from diagnosis of 100 patients with congestive heart failure. By the third year, 60 patients have been censored. Which of the following would not be a reason for one of these patients being censored?
opts: The patient died of another cause before year 3.

This patient can be censored. Someone who dies of a cause unrelated to the outcome being followed leaves observation without having had the event of interest, so the patient is counted only for the time observed before that death.
The patient decided not to continue in the study.
This patient is censored. A patient who decides to leave the study is no longer observed, so their survival after that point is unknown and they are counted only for the time they were followed.
The patient had been enrolled in the study for less than 3 years.

This patient is censored. Someone enrolled for less than 3 years has not yet been followed as long as the analysis time, so their survival to year 3 is unknown at analysis and they count only for the time observed.
The patient developed another disease that could be fatal.

Correct. Developing another potentially fatal disease does not remove anyone from observation. Patients are censored when they leave the study or have not been followed for the full period; a patient who has another disease but is still alive and being followed remains in the analysis.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.6

questions.q: Which of the following kinds of studies cannot be used to identify prognostic factors?
opts: Prevalence study

Correct. A prevalence study assesses a population for a condition at one point in time, so it measures no events over time. Prognosis is about outcomes of disease over time, so this design cannot identify prognostic factors (prevalence studies are also poor for cause and effect and better for developing hypotheses).
Time-to-event analysis

Time-to-event analysis can identify prognostic factors. Cox proportional hazards regression can find prognostic indicators of survival in a given disease, taking into account the effects of several predictors on the survival curve.
Case-control study

A case-control study can be used to look for prognostic factors, because patients who had the outcome can be compared with patients who did not for earlier characteristics. It is not the design that fails; the prevalence study is, since it measures no events over time.
Cohort study
A cohort study can identify prognostic factors. Patients are followed over time from zero time, and the factors present at the start are compared between those who do and do not develop the outcome.
questions.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.7

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the information in a survival curve?
opts: An unbiased estimate of survival even if some patients leave the study

A survival curve does not guarantee an unbiased estimate. Patients who leave the study (migration) can bias the curve if they differ from those who stay, and the more dropouts, the greater the potential for bias.
The estimated probability of survival from zero time

Correct. A survival curve gives the estimated probability of surviving to any point in time, calculated from the cumulative probability of surviving each preceding interval, starting at zero time. It estimates survival for a hypothetical rather than an actual cohort.
The proportion of a cohort still alive at the end of follow-up

The curve does not simply report the proportion of the original cohort alive at the end of follow-up. It is an estimate built interval by interval that accounts for patients who left the study, and it shows survival at every point in time rather than only at the end.
The rate at which original members of the cohort leave the study
The curve shows deaths (events) over time, not how fast members leave the study. Patients who leave are taken into account in the estimate, but their departure rate is not what is plotted.
The cumulative survival of a cohort over time

A survival curve does track survival cumulatively, so this is close, but it is not the best description. The curve gives the estimated probability of surviving from zero time, built interval by interval and adjusted for patients who left, and it estimates survival for a hypothetical rather than an actual cohort, so it is not a direct count of the actual cohort's survivors.
