questions.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate sample for a study of prognosis?
opts: Members of the general population

The general population is mostly people who do not have the disease, whereas prognosis studies follow people who already have it, so this sample does not describe the course of illness for a specific group of patients. The best sample depends on who will use the results.
Patients in primary care in the community

Patients in primary care are right if the results will be used by primary care clinicians, but this sample would not describe the prognosis of patients seen at specialist centers, so it is not always the most appropriate.
Patients admitted to a community hospital

Patients admitted to a community hospital represent one referral pattern and one setting. They fit users of that setting, but they may differ from patients in primary care or at referral centers, so this is not the best sample in every case.
Patients referred to a specialist

Patients referred to a specialist are a selected group whose referral pattern differs from community care. They suit specialist users, but results from academic or referral centers may not apply to patients seen elsewhere.
It depends on who will use the results of the study.

Correct. The right sample depends on the question: referral pattern (academic medical center versus community) affects who is in the study, and results apply only to patients similar to those the reader sees. Prognosis in primary care and among those referred to specialists are both useful to know.

questions.q: Investigators wish to describe the clinical course of multiple sclerosis. They take advantage of a clinical trial, already completed, in which control patients received usual care. Patients in the trial had been identified at referral centers, had been enrolled at the time of diagnosis, and had met rigorous entry criteria. After 10 years, all patients had been examined yearly and remained under observation, and 40% were still able to walk. Which of the following most limits the credibility of this study?
opts: Inconsistent zero time
Zero time was consistent here. Patients were enrolled at the time of diagnosis, so all were counted from a similar point in the disease course, which is what an inception cohort requires.
Generalizability

Correct. Patients had to meet stringent trial entry criteria at referral centers, so the usual-care patients are not representative of people with multiple sclerosis in the general population or in a defined clinical setting. Generalizability is often limited because study patients may not be representative of other populations.
Measurement bias

Nothing in the study suggests measurement bias. All patients were examined yearly in the same way, so no group had a greater chance of outcome detection, and walking ability is a straightforward outcome.
Migration bias
Migration bias is not the problem here. All patients remained under observation for 10 years, so no dropouts changed the composition of the cohort.
Failure to use time-to-event methods

With every patient examined yearly and observed for the full 10 years, there were no incomplete-follow-up problems that time-to-event methods exist to handle. The main limitation is who was studied, not how the results were analyzed.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.10

questions.q: A cohort study is done to assess how often headaches are present in children who have had concussions. At the scheduled 5-year follow-up, one- fifth of the participants have dropped out of the study. The investigators consider calculating the incidence of headaches using multiple imputation. Which of the following is correct?
opts: Multiple imputation assumes that the characteristics measured in the study can be used to reliably estimate the missing values.

Correct. Multiple imputation is a technique for estimating missing values by statistical modeling of the patients with complete data, taking their other characteristics into account. It therefore assumes that the measured characteristics can reliably predict what is missing.
Multiple imputation removes the effects of bias from incomplete follow-up.
Imputation does not remove the effects of bias. If patients who dropped out differ from those who stayed in ways that the measured characteristics do not capture, the estimates can still be biased.
Multiple imputation can estimate headache rates for the missing patients by randomly selecting whether headache is present in patients with complete follow- up.

Imputation does not simply pick headache present or absent at random from patients with complete follow-up. It builds a statistical model from complete cases and other characteristics to estimate the missing values; a simple average of measured values is a cruder and likely biased approach.
Complete case analysis compares the results for patients with complete information to results for those with missing values.

Complete case analysis uses only patients with complete information and leaves out those with missing values; it does not compare the two groups. Excluding dropouts can bias results, which is why imputation is considered.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.11

questions.q: Many different clinical prediction rules have been developed to assess the severity of community-acquired pneumonia. Which of the following is the most important reason for choosing one to use?
opts: The prediction rule classifies patients into groups with very different prognosis.

Separating patients into groups with very different prognosis is a desirable feature, but a rule can do this in the patients it was built on and still fail elsewhere. That is why testing in other patients matters more.
The prediction rule has been validated in different settings.

Correct. Even a rule built with the best methods is most strongly tested by showing that it predicts outcomes in patients other than those used to develop it. Study patients must be similar to your own for a rule to apply, so validation in different settings is the most important reason.
Many variables are included in the rule.
The number of variables is not the measure of a good rule. Multiple factors predict better than a single data point, but including many variables does not show that the rule works in other patients.
Prognostic factors include state-of-the-science diagnostic tests.

Using state-of-the-science diagnostic tests does not show that a rule predicts well. Rules are more practical when they rely on readily available clinical data, and what demonstrates that a rule works is that it predicts outcomes in patients other than those used to develop it.
The score is calculated using computers.
How the score is calculated is a convenience, not evidence of accuracy. A rule may be simple to compute by hand or by computer, but only testing in other patients shows whether it predicts well.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.12

questions.q: In a study of patients who smoke and developed peripheral arterial disease, the hazard ratio for amputation in patients who continued to smoke, relative to those who quit smoking, is 5. Which of the following best characterizes the hazard ratio?
opts: In this study, it is the rate of continued smoking divided by the rate of quitting.

The hazard ratio here is not the ratio of the rates of smoking and quitting. It compares the rate of the outcome, amputation, in the two groups: patients who continued to smoke relative to those who quit.
It can be estimated from a case-control study of smoking and amputation.

A case-control study measures exposure between cases and controls and yields an odds ratio. A hazard ratio comes from following patients over time in a survival analysis, which needs time-to-event information that a case-control study does not provide.
It cannot be adjusted for the presence or absence of other factors related to prognosis.
A hazard ratio can be adjusted. Cox proportional hazards regression studies the effect of an exposure on outcome after adjusting for confounders and for other factors related to prognosis.
It conveys information similar to relative risk.

Correct. The hazard ratio from a Cox survival analysis can be interpreted like a relative risk: a ratio of 5 means patients who continued to smoke have five times the risk of amputation compared with those who quit; a ratio below 1 would mean protection.
It is calculated from the cumulative incidence of amputation in smokers and quitters.

A hazard ratio compares the rate at which the event occurs over time in the two groups, estimated with survival analysis, rather than dividing the proportions who had the outcome. A ratio of cumulative incidences is a relative risk, which is similar to a hazard ratio but not identical.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.13

questions.q: In a time-to-event analyses, the event:
opts: Can occur only once
This statement is true but incomplete. An outcome in time-to-event analysis occurs only once, but it is also either/or, so the best answer includes both features.
Is dichotomous
This statement is true but incomplete. The event is dichotomous, occurring or not, but it also can happen only once (death, first recurrence), so the best answer includes both features.
Both A and B
Correct. The outcome event in a time-to-event analysis is dichotomous (it occurs or it does not, such as living versus dying) and it can occur only once, so both statements are true.
Neither A nor B
This is incorrect, because both statements are true. The event is either/or and it occurs only once for each patient.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 17; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 49; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 8.14

questions.q: A randomized controlled trial compares two drugs in common use for the treatment of asthma. Three hundred patients were entered into the trial, and eligibility criteria were broad. No effort was made to blind patients to their treatment group after enrollment. Except for the study drugs, care was decided by each individual physician and patient. The outcome measure was a brief questionnaire assessing asthma-related quality of life. Which of the following best describes this trial?
opts: Pragmatic trial

Correct. This trial was built to mirror everyday practice: two drugs already in common use, broad eligibility, no blinding after enrollment, usual care for everything except the study drugs, and a patient-centered questionnaire outcome. That is a pragmatic trial, which asks whether a treatment works under ordinary circumstances.
Large simple trial

A large simple trial needs a very large number of participants with minimal data collection, and this trial enrolled only three hundred patients. Its real-world design features make it pragmatic, not large.
Efficacy trial

An efficacy trial tests a treatment under ideal circumstances, typically with narrow eligibility, tight control of care, and blinding. This trial deliberately did the opposite (broad eligibility, usual care, no blinding), so its results speak to effectiveness in ordinary circumstances.
Equivalence trial

An equivalence trial is designed to show that two treatments have effects that are essentially the same. Nothing in this trial is built around proving sameness; its defining features concern how closely it resembles real-world care.
Noninferiority trial

A noninferiority trial asks whether a new treatment is unlikely to be less effective than an established one, usually because the new one is cheaper, safer, or easier. Here both drugs are already in common use and no new-versus-established question is posed; the design features describe a pragmatic trial.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.1

questions.q: A randomized controlled trial compared angioplasty with fibrinolysis for the treatment of acute myocardial infarction. The authors state that “analysis was by intention to treat.” Which of the following is an advantage of this approach?
opts: It describes the effects of treatments that patients have actually received.

Describing the effects of treatments patients actually received is the opposite of intention-to-treat analysis, which counts patients in the group they were randomized to. Analysis by treatment actually received is a per-protocol or as-treated analysis, which is not protected by randomization.
It is unlikely to underestimate treatment effect.

Intention-to-treat analysis does not protect against underestimating the effect. When patients assigned to a treatment do not take it, or cross over, the two groups become more alike and the measured difference shrinks toward no effect.
It is not affected by patients dropping out of the study.

Intention-to-treat analysis is affected by dropouts. Patients who stop treatment stay in their assigned group, which dilutes the observed difference. What intention-to-treat does is keep everyone in the analysis rather than dropping them.
It describes the consequences of offering treatments regardless of whether they are actually taken.

Correct. Patients are analyzed according to the group they were randomized to, so the result shows the consequences of offering a treatment, whether or not patients take it. This reflects effectiveness in ordinary circumstances, where compliance is imperfect.
It describes whether treatment can work under ideal circumstances.

Effects under ideal circumstances describe efficacy, where everyone takes the treatment as intended. Intention-to-treat analysis includes the noncompliance and dropouts of real life, so it addresses effectiveness rather than efficacy.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.2

questions.q: In a randomized trial, patients with meningitis who were treated with corticosteroids had lower rates of death, hearing loss, and neurologic sequelae. Which of the following is a randomized comparison?
opts: The subset of patients who, at the time of randomization, were severely affected by the disease

Correct. Severity at the time of randomization is a characteristic that existed before treatment was assigned, so it was randomly allocated to both groups and comparing the severely affected patients in each group remains a randomized comparison. Randomization balances characteristics present at the start, not those that arise afterward.
Patients who experienced other treatments versus those who did not

Whether patients experienced other treatments is decided after randomization by clinicians and patients, not by chance. Groups formed this way can differ in prognosis for reasons unrelated to the drug, so this is an observational comparison subject to confounding.
Patients who remained in the trial versus those who dropped out after randomization

Staying in the trial or dropping out happens after randomization and is related to how patients are doing and to side effects. The two groups formed by retention differ in more than chance, so this is not a randomized comparison.
Patients who responded to the drug versus those who did not

Response to the drug develops after randomization and depends on patient characteristics such as disease biology and severity. Responders and nonresponders were not randomly allocated, so comparing them reintroduces confounding.
Patients who took the drug compared with those who did not

Taking the drug (compliance) is a behavior that arises after randomization, and patients who take medication often differ from those who do not in health, motivation, and other prognostic factors. Only the comparison of assigned groups is protected by randomization.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.3

questions.q: A patient asks for your advice about whether to begin an exercise program to reduce his risk of sudden death. You look for randomized controlled trials but find only observational studies about this question. Some are cohort studies comparing sudden death rates in exercisers with rates of sudden death in sedentary people; others are case control studies comparing exercise patterns in people who had experienced sudden death and matched controls. Which of the following is not an advantage of observational studies of treatments like these over randomized controlled trials?
opts: Reported effects are for patients who have actually experienced the intervention.

This is a genuine advantage of observational studies. They collect information on patients who are actually being treated in practice, whereas a randomized trial is usually analyzed by assigned group, which includes patients who never took the intervention.
It may be possible to carry out these studies by using existing data that was collected for other purposes.

This is a genuine advantage of observational studies. They can be done with records and data already collected for other purposes, which avoids the cost and logistics of enrolling, randomizing, and following participants prospectively.
The results can be generalized to more ordinary, real-world settings.

This is a genuine advantage of observational studies. They involve real-world patients in real-world settings, so the results are more readily generalized to ordinary practice than the results of a tightly controlled trial with narrow eligibility.
Treatment groups would have had a similar prognosis except for treatment itself.

Correct, this is not an advantage of observational studies. Without randomization, people who choose or receive a treatment tend to differ in prognosis from those who do not, so confounding is difficult to avoid. Creating groups with similar prognosis except for treatment is the advantage of randomization.
A large sample size is easier to achieve.

This is a genuine advantage of observational studies. Randomized trials are expensive and logistically demanding (sample selection, randomization, blinding, time), whereas observational designs can more easily reach a large sample.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.4

questions.q: In a randomized controlled trial of a program to reduce lower extremity problems in patients with diabetes mellitus, patients were excluded if they were younger than age 40, were diagnosed before becoming 30 years old, took specific medication for hyperglycemia, had other serious illness or disability, or were not compliant with prescribed treatment during a run-in period. Which of the following is an advantage of this approach?
opts: It makes it possible to do an intention-to-treat analysis.

Intention-to-treat analysis is a choice about how to analyze the data (by randomized group) and is possible whatever the eligibility criteria. Restricting who enters the trial does not create or enable it.
It avoids selection bias.

Strict eligibility does not avoid selection; it deliberately creates a narrower, selected group of patients. That makes the patients more alike and helps internal validity, but the trial patients differ from typical patients, so generalizability falls. Randomization is what handles differences in prognosis between the treatment groups.
It improves the generalizability of the study.

Strict exclusion criteria reduce generalizability. Excluding younger patients, early-onset disease, other serious illness, and patients who were noncompliant during the run-in period means the trial patients do not represent the wider population that clinicians treat.
It makes an effectiveness trial possible.

An effectiveness trial reflects ordinary circumstances, which calls for broad eligibility and typical patients. Excluding people who are ill, disabled, or noncompliant is characteristic of an efficacy trial that tests the program under favorable conditions.
It improves the internal validity of the study.

Correct. Strict inclusion and exclusion criteria (and a compliance run-in) make trial patients more alike and more likely to follow the program, so a real difference between treatments is easier to detect. That improves internal validity, the degree results are correct for the patients studied, at the cost of generalizability.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 25; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.5

questions.q: Which of the following is not accomplished by an intention-to-treat analysis?
opts: A comparison of the effects of offering the experimental treatments

Intention-to-treat analysis does accomplish this. Because patients are analyzed in the group they were assigned to, it compares the effects of offering one treatment with offering the other, whether or not patients accept it.
A comparison more relevant to effectiveness questions

Intention-to-treat analysis does accomplish this. Since it includes the noncompliance, crossover, and dropouts that occur in ordinary practice, it addresses effectiveness (whether a treatment works in ordinary circumstances) rather than efficacy under ideal conditions.
A comparison of the effects of actually taking the experimental treatments

Correct, this is not accomplished. Intention-to-treat analysis compares groups by assignment, so it does not isolate the effect of actually taking treatment. Studying patients by the treatment they really took treats the data like a cohort study, which is vulnerable to confounding.
A randomized comparison of treatment effects

Intention-to-treat analysis does accomplish this. Groups are kept as they were formed by randomization, so the comparison keeps the protection against confounding that randomization gives, unlike comparisons based on who took the drug.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.6

questions.q: You are reading a report of a randomized controlled trial and wonder whether stratified randomization, which the trial used, was likely to improve internal validity. For which of the following is stratified randomization particularly helpful?
opts: The study includes many patients.

A large number of patients does not make stratification especially helpful; with large samples, simple randomization is more likely to balance characteristics by chance. Stratification matters more when the trial is small enough that chance imbalance is a worry.
One of the baseline variables is strongly related to prognosis.

Correct. When a baseline characteristic is strongly related to prognosis, stratified randomization first divides patients by that characteristic and then randomizes within each stratum, guaranteeing both treatment groups have similar mixes of it. It is most useful for this and for smaller trials, where simple randomization might leave groups with different prognosis.
Assignment to treatment group is not blinded.

Whether assignment is blinded concerns allocation concealment and blinding, which protect against knowledge of the assignment influencing enrollment, care, or assessment. Stratification balances baseline characteristics and does nothing about blinding.
Many patients are expected to drop out.
Dropouts arise after randomization and threaten complete follow-up. Stratified randomization balances baseline characteristics at the start and cannot prevent or offset later losses.
An intention-to-treat analysis is planned.

Planning an intention-to-treat analysis is a decision about analysis, which counts patients by assigned group. It does not depend on stratification and is not the situation where stratified randomization is particularly helpful.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.7

questions.q: A randomized controlled trial is analyzed according to the treatment each patient actually received. Which of the following best describes this approach to analysis?
opts: Superiority

Superiority describes the goal of a trial, which is to determine whether one treatment is better than another. It says nothing about whether patients are analyzed by treatment received or by assigned group.
Intention-to-treat
Intention-to-treat analysis is the opposite approach: patients are analyzed in the group they were randomized to, regardless of the treatment they actually received.
Noninferiority
Noninferiority describes a trial goal, which is to show that a new treatment is not unacceptably worse than an established one. It is not a way of assigning outcomes to treatment groups.
Open label
Open label means no blinding is done, so participants and investigators know the treatment. It describes knowledge of treatment assignment, not how outcomes are attributed in the analysis.
Per-protocol

Correct. In a per-protocol analysis, outcomes are attributed to the treatment patients actually received rather than the group they were randomized to. Because who takes treatment is no longer random, it loses randomization's protection against confounding.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 9.8

questions.q: In a randomized controlled trial, a beta-blocking drug is found to be more effective than placebo for stage fright. Patients taking the beta-blocker tended to have a lower pulse rate and to feel more lethargic, which are known effects of this drug. For which of the following is blinding possible?
opts: The patients' physicians

Physicians caring for patients would notice the lower pulse rate and lethargy that the beta-blocker causes, which reveals who is taking the active drug. Even when blinded at the start, treatment effects and side effects can unmask the treatment group.
The investigators who assigned patients to treatment groups

Correct. The investigators who assign patients to groups make that decision before any drug is started, so no side effect can reveal the assignment to them. This is allocation concealment, in which the people assigning patients are kept unaware of which treatment comes next.
The patients in the trial

Patients would notice a slower pulse and lethargy, known effects of the drug, and could figure out that they are taking the beta-blocker rather than the placebo. Side effects can defeat blinding even when it was intended.
The investigators who assess outcome

Blinding outcome assessors is often possible and is a standard way to limit biased assessment, for example by having them review coded records. But assessing outcomes here means observing patients after treatment begins, and the slower pulse and lethargy can reveal who is on the drug, so only the people assigning treatment, who act before any drug is given, are certain to stay unaware.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes “equipoise” as the rationale for a randomized trial of two drugs?
opts: The drugs are known to be equally effective.

If the drugs were known to be equally effective, there would be conclusive evidence about the comparison and nothing left to test. Equipoise means genuine uncertainty about which is better, not knowledge that they are the same.
One of the drugs is known to be more toxic.

Equipoise means genuine uncertainty about which drug is better overall. Knowing only that one drug is more toxic does not establish that it is equally good or worse; and if the evidence already showed it to be worse overall, randomizing patients to it would be unethical. Either way, the choice does not describe the state of uncertainty that justifies a trial.
Neither drug is known to be more effective than the other.

Correct. Equipoise means the scientific community has no conclusive evidence that either drug is better; there may be opinions and partial evidence, but no consensus. Randomization is ethical only in this state of uncertainty, and the trial is done to resolve it.
Although one drug is more effective, the other drug is easier to take with fewer side effects.

If one drug were known to be more effective, patients randomized to the other would be denied a treatment known to work better. That is conclusive evidence about efficacy, so this is not equipoise, even though the other drug's convenience and side effects may matter.

questions.q: Antibiotic A is the established treatment for community-acquired pneumonia, but it is expensive and has many side effects. A new drug, antibiotic B, has just been developed for community-acquired pneumonia and is less expensive and has fewer side effects, but its efficacy, relative to drug A, is not well established. Which of the following would be the best kind of trial for evaluating drug B?
opts: Superiority

A superiority trial tries to show that one treatment is better than another. Antibiotic B is cheaper and has fewer side effects, and the goal is to show it is not worse, so the question is not whether B is better in efficacy.
Crossover

Crossover refers to participants moving from one randomly assigned treatment to another. It describes how patients move between treatments, not the question of whether a new drug is no worse than the established drug.
Cluster

Cluster refers to selecting or assigning whole groups (for example hospital units) instead of individual patients. It concerns how participants are grouped and does not address whether antibiotic B is no less effective than A.
Noninferiority

Correct. A noninferiority trial determines whether a new treatment is unlikely to be less effective than an established one. It fits antibiotic B, which has advantages (cheaper, fewer side effects) but whose efficacy relative to antibiotic A is not established. It usually needs a larger sample size than a superiority trial because differences may be small.
Equivalence

An equivalence trial aims to show the two drugs are essentially the same in both directions. For antibiotic B, the important question is whether it is no worse than A, since better or equal efficacy plus lower cost and fewer side effects would be acceptable, which is the noninferiority question.

questions.q: In a randomized controlled trial of two drugs for coronary artery disease, the primary outcome is a composite of acute myocardial infarction, severe angina pectoris, and cardiac death. Which of the following is the main advantage of this approach?
opts: There are more outcomes events than there would be for any of the individual outcomes.

Correct. Combining related, clinically important outcomes produces more outcome events than any single outcome would, which increases the trial's ability to detect a real effect if one exists. The drawback is that the intervention may affect components differently, and the composite can mask this.
All outcomes are equally affected by the interventions.

The interventions may affect the components differently; one outcome may improve while another does not or worsens. That is the main disadvantage of a composite, which can hide differing effects, so it is not an advantage.
The trial has more generalizability.
Combining outcomes does not affect generalizability, which depends on how representative the patients and setting are. A composite outcome changes the number of events, not who is studied.
Each of the individual outcomes is important in its own right.

Each component having clinical importance is a requirement for a sensible composite, so that the combination is meaningful. It is not the advantage of combining them; the advantage is the larger total number of events.
If one outcome is infrequent, others make up for it.

This misstates the benefit. Pooling outcomes adds up events to give the trial more power, but a frequent outcome does not substitute for an infrequent one in interpretation: the composite can hide that individual components respond differently, so the infrequent outcome's own effect remains unknown.

questions.q: In a randomized controlled trial comparing two approaches to managing children with bronchiolitis, baseline characteristics of the 200 children in the trial are somewhat different in the two randomly allocated groups. Which of the following might explain this finding?
opts: “Bad luck” in randomization

Chance can produce imbalance between randomly allocated groups, especially in smaller trials, so this is a possible explanation. But it is not the only one, since a breakdown in allocation concealment can also produce imbalanced groups.
A breakdown in allocation concealment

A breakdown in allocation concealment (by poor methods or cheating) lets those assigning patients steer them into groups, which would show up as baseline differences, so it is a possible explanation. But chance imbalance is also possible, so this alone is incomplete.
Both

Correct. Bad luck in randomization and a breakdown in allocation concealment can each leave baseline characteristics different between the groups. Small differences are expected by chance; the challenge is deciding how large a difference must be to raise concern.
Neither

Some baseline differences are expected with random allocation, and concealment failures also cause them. Ruling out both would mean expecting groups to be identical, which randomization does not promise, especially with only two hundred children.

questions.q: Which of the following is usually learned from a Phase III drug trial?
opts: The relationship between dose and efficacy

The relationship between dose and efficacy is examined in Phase II trials, which involve a small number of participants and identify preliminary effect and any relationship to dose. Phase III trials aim at definitive evidence of effect.
Rates of uncommon side effects
Uncommon side effects are usually not identified in Phase III trials. They are detected by postmarketing surveillance, which follows large numbers of patients after the drug is released.
Efficacy or effectiveness

Correct. Phase III trials are larger, randomized trials intended to give definitive evidence of efficacy or effectiveness and identify some common side effects. These are the trials usually published in the clinical literature.
The dose range that is well tolerated
The dose range that is well tolerated is worked out in Phase I trials, which use a small number of participants without a control group to identify a safe, tolerated dose.

questions.q: Which of the following is the main advantage of randomized controlled trials over observational studies of treatment effects?
opts: Fewer ethical challenges

Randomized controlled trials have more ethical challenges, not fewer, because investigators assign treatments by chance. That is acceptable only with genuine uncertainty about which treatment is better, with participant consent, and with stopping the study if harm, futility, or benefit becomes evident.
Prevention of confounding

Correct. Randomization creates groups that would have the same outcome rates, on average, were it not for the treatment, so confounding is prevented. In observational studies, systematic differences in groups other than the treatment factor make confounding difficult to avoid; this is why randomized trials are the gold standard for treatment efficacy.
Resemble usual care

Whether a trial resembles usual care depends on its design; observational studies of patients currently being treated are the ones that naturally reflect real-world care. It is not an inherent advantage of randomized trials.
Quicker answer

Randomized controlled trials are not quicker; they involve logistical issues such as sample selection, randomization, blinding, consistency across participants, and time. An observational study using existing data can often give an answer sooner.
Less expensive

Randomized controlled trials are more expensive, not less, because of the logistics of recruiting, randomizing, blinding, and following participants. Their cost is accepted because of what they prevent, which is confounding.

questions.q:
A study was conducted to determine whether a fecal occult blood screening test reduced mortality from colorectal cancer. People of ages 50 to 60 years were randomized to the screening test or to a control group and followed for 13 years. Over this time, there were 323 cancer cases and 82 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,570 people randomized to annual screening; there were 356 cancers and 121 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,394 people randomized to the control group. Investigators found that for dried stool cards the sensitivity was 80% and the specificity 98%. If the cards were rehydrated, sensitivity improved to 90% and specificity decreased to 90%.

What is the relative risk reduction of colorectal mortality in the screened group?
opts: Correct. Death risk was 82/15,570 = 0.0053 with screening and 121/15,394 = 0.0079 in the control group. The absolute risk reduction is 0.0026, and dividing by the control-group risk gives 0.0026/0.0079 = 0.33, so screening cut colorectal cancer mortality by about 33% (equivalently 1 minus the relative risk of 0.67).

This is not what the risk figures give. Subtracting the death counts gives 121 - 82 = 39 fewer deaths, but that is a count, not a percentage. The relative reduction divides the risk difference (0.0026) by the control-group risk (0.0079) and equals about 33%.

A figure near 48% to 49% comes from dividing the risk difference (0.0026) by the screened group's risk (0.0053) instead of the control group's risk (0.0079). The reference group for a reduction is the control group, which gives about 33%.

questions.q:
A study was conducted to determine whether a fecal occult blood screening test reduced mortality from colorectal cancer. People of ages 50 to 60 years were randomized to the screening test or to a control group and followed for 13 years. Over this time, there were 323 cancer cases and 82 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,570 people randomized to annual screening; there were 356 cancers and 121 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,394 people randomized to the control group. Investigators found that for dried stool cards the sensitivity was 80% and the specificity 98%. If the cards were rehydrated, sensitivity improved to 90% and specificity decreased to 90%.

How many patients would you need to screen over the next 13 years to prevent one death from colorectal cancer?
opts: This is the reciprocal of something else. About 43 is 15,394/356, the number of control-group people per cancer case (cancer incidence, not death from colorectal cancer). The number needed to screen for one fewer death uses the difference in death risk between groups, which gives about 385.

This is not the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction. The reciprocal of the screened group's death risk (1/0.0053) is only about 190, and that describes deaths within one group. The prevention effect is the difference between the groups (0.0079 - 0.0053 = 0.0026), whose reciprocal is about 385.

Correct. The number needed to screen is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction: the difference in death risk is 0.0079 - 0.0053 = 0.0026, and 1/0.0026 is about 385 people screened over 13 years to prevent one death from colorectal cancer. A large number like this means many people are screened for each one who benefits.

questions.q:
A study was conducted to determine whether a fecal occult blood screening test reduced mortality from colorectal cancer. People of ages 50 to 60 years were randomized to the screening test or to a control group and followed for 13 years. Over this time, there were 323 cancer cases and 82 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,570 people randomized to annual screening; there were 356 cancers and 121 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,394 people randomized to the control group. Investigators found that for dried stool cards the sensitivity was 80% and the specificity 98%. If the cards were rehydrated, sensitivity improved to 90% and specificity decreased to 90%.

If rehydrated instead of dried stool cards were used:
opts: Screened patients would need fewer colonoscopies.

Rehydration lowers specificity from 98% to 90%, so the false-positive rate rises from 2% to 10% (about 20 versus 100 false positives per 1,000 people without cancer). More false positives means more people sent for colonoscopy, not fewer.
The positive predictive value would increase.

Positive predictive value falls, not rises. The positive likelihood ratio drops from 0.80/0.02 = 40 to 0.90/0.10 = 9. At a 1% cancer prevalence, the chance that a positive test means cancer falls from about 29% to about 8%, because many more false positives dilute the true positives.
The probability of disease with a negative test would decrease.

Correct. Sensitivity rises from 80% to 90%, so there are fewer false negatives, and the negative likelihood ratio drops from 0.20 to about 0.11. At any given prevalence the chance of disease after a negative test therefore falls (at 1% prevalence, from about 0.21% to about 0.11%). The price is lower specificity, more false positives, and more colonoscopies.

questions.q:
In a randomized controlled trial of screening chest x-rays and sputum cytology for lung cancer, approximately 9,000 men were randomized to screening for 6 years or a control group. After 20 years, the lung cancer mortality was the same in both groups (4.4/1,000 person-years in the screened group and 3.9/1,000 person-years in the control group). However, the median survival for patients diagnosed with lung cancer was 1.3 years in the screened group and 0.9 years in the control group. Also, screening found more lung cancer—206 cancers were diagnosed in the screened group and 160 in the control group.

What is the best conclusion after reading such a study?
opts: Finding a better survival rate but not a change in the mortality rate of lung cancer makes no sense and the study must be flawed.

The pattern is not a flaw. Longer survival measured from diagnosis together with unchanged mortality is exactly what lead-time bias produces: earlier detection starts the survival clock sooner without delaying death. Here mortality was 4.4 versus 3.9 per 1,000 person-years, so mortality gave no sign of benefit.
Because mortality did not change, screening may have resulted in more “disease time” for those diagnosed with lung cancer.

Correct. Screening moves the date of diagnosis earlier (lead time), so patients live longer after diagnosis, which is more 'disease time', without dying later. Because mortality did not fall in a randomized trial, the better survival is likely lead-time bias (overdiagnosis is another possible cause), not real benefit.
Improved survival demonstrates screening was effective in the study.

Improved survival from the time of diagnosis does not show screening worked. Survival counted from diagnosis can lengthen simply because the diagnosis was made earlier (lead-time bias), or because screening found cancers that would never have mattered (overdiagnosis). Effectiveness requires better outcomes such as lower mortality, and mortality was not lower here.

questions.q:
In a randomized controlled trial of screening chest x-rays and sputum cytology for lung cancer, approximately 9,000 men were randomized to screening for 6 years or a control group. After 20 years, the lung cancer mortality was the same in both groups (4.4/1,000 person-years in the screened group and 3.9/1,000 person-years in the control group). However, the median survival for patients diagnosed with lung cancer was 1.3 years in the screened group and 0.9 years in the control group. Also, screening found more lung cancer—206 cancers were diagnosed in the screened group and 160 in the control group.

What bias is the best explanation for the improved survival in the face of no improvement in the mortality rate in this study?
opts: Lead-time bias

Correct. Lead time is the interval between detection by screening and when the cancer would have been diagnosed from symptoms. Survival counted from diagnosis grows by that interval even when the date of death is unchanged, which matches better survival with no change in mortality.
Survival bias

Survival bias is not one of the biases named for screening studies (lead-time, length-time and compliance bias). The pattern here, longer survival counted from diagnosis with unchanged mortality, is the signature of earlier diagnosis, which is lead-time bias.
Compliance bias

Compliance bias arises when volunteers who accept screening are more health-conscious and do better, and it is a problem in observational studies. Here people were randomized to screening or control, so group differences in compliance do not explain the survival gap.
Length-time bias

Length-time bias arises because screening preferentially finds slow-growing, better-prognosis cancers. It can contribute, but it is not the best single explanation here: the best-fit explanation is that earlier diagnosis simply lengthened the time from diagnosis to death (lead time).

questions.q:
In a randomized controlled trial of screening chest x-rays and sputum cytology for lung cancer, approximately 9,000 men were randomized to screening for 6 years or a control group. After 20 years, the lung cancer mortality was the same in both groups (4.4/1,000 person-years in the screened group and 3.9/1,000 person-years in the control group). However, the median survival for patients diagnosed with lung cancer was 1.3 years in the screened group and 0.9 years in the control group. Also, screening found more lung cancer—206 cancers were diagnosed in the screened group and 160 in the control group.

What is the most likely reason for the fact that 206 lung cancers were found in the screened group and only 160 in the control group?
opts: There were more smokers in the screened group.
Randomization spreads smoking and other risk factors about evenly between the groups, so a chance excess of smokers is an unlikely reason for 206 versus 160 cancers in a trial of about 9,000 men.
Screening found cancers earlier and the number of cancers in the control group will catch up over time.

If screening only found cancers earlier, the control group would catch up as its patients developed symptoms. Even after 20 years the control group still had fewer cancers (160 versus 206), so the extra cancers were not simply diagnosed sooner.
Screening picked up some cancers that would not have come to medical attention without screening.

Correct. Overdiagnosis means detecting disease that would never have caused symptoms or needed treatment. The screened group kept more cancers even after 20 years, so screening found cancers that would never have come to medical attention on their own; finding them does not help the patient.

questions.q: Researchers in Denmark looked at the incidence of breast cancer over 3 decades in areas of the country where mammogram screening was introduced compared to locations where screening was not offered. Small invasive cancers (<2 cm) were found more frequently in the screened group, but the incidence of large invasive cancers (>2 cm) was similar for the screened and unscreened groups. These findings remained after controlling for age differences. Which of the following is true?
opts: If lead-time bias is present, both cancer survival rates and cancer mortality rates will be lower in the screening group.

This statement is false. With lead-time bias, survival counted from diagnosis looks longer because diagnosis happens earlier, but the date of death does not change, so cancer mortality rates are unchanged, not lower.
Many of the smaller tumors detected may not have become clinically significant

Correct. More small invasive cancers in screened areas with no change in large invasive cancers suggests overdiagnosis: some small tumors detected would never have become clinically significant. Finding disease that does not help the patient is the overdiagnosis problem.
Overdiagnosis is not present because the cancers found were invasive.

This statement is false. Overdiagnosis means detecting disease that would never have caused symptoms or harm, and a cancer can be invasive on pathology yet so slow-growing that it never matters in the person's lifetime. Being invasive does not rule overdiagnosis out.
The study does not account for possible changes in the cancer incidence over time.

This statement is not accurate for this design. The study compared screened areas with unscreened areas over the same three decades, so background changes in cancer incidence over time affect both groups and are not what separates them.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23; 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 10.7

questions.q: A review compared the performance of HPV testing versus cytology (pap smears) for cervical cancer screening. Compared to cytology, HPV testing had better detection of precancerous lesions that would be treated to prevent subsequent cancers. However, it also had a higher false-positive rate. Which of the following is incorrect?
opts: HPV is more sensitive than cytology for screening.

This statement is true, so it is not the exception. The review found HPV testing detected more precancerous lesions, which is higher sensitivity (a higher percentage of people with lesions test positive).
HPV is less specific than cytology for screening.
This statement is true, so it is not the exception. A higher false-positive rate means lower specificity, because specificity is the proportion of people without lesions who test negative.
More frequent testing may improve the sensitivity of cytology.

This statement is true, so it is not the exception. Repeating a test gives more chances to detect a lesion that an earlier test missed, so repeated cytology raises its sensitivity (at the cost of more false positives, so lower specificity).
The positive predictive value is higher for HPV than cytology.

Correct, this is the incorrect statement. Positive predictive value is true positives divided by all positives. HPV testing adds true positives through higher sensitivity but adds more false positives through lower specificity, and the extra false positives outweigh the gain, so at a given prevalence its positive predictive value is lower than for cytology, not higher. Its higher sensitivity gives it the better negative predictive value.

questions.q: When assessing a new vaccine, which of the following is least important:
opts: Efficacy in preventing the disease

Efficacy is central: a vaccine that does not prevent the disease has no purpose. Efficacy asks whether it works under ideal conditions, and effectiveness asks whether it works in everyday practice; both are essential.
Safety of the vaccine
Safety is central: giving a vaccine to healthy people is only justified if harms are small, and adverse effects are studied with longitudinal follow-up. Safety is always weighed against benefit.
Danger of the disease
The danger of the disease (burden of suffering, such as mortality and hospitalizations) is a core reason to include a condition in preventive care. A mild or rare disease may not justify a vaccine.
Cost of giving the vaccine

Correct. Cost matters, but it is only one component of a cost-effectiveness analysis, which also depends on efficacy, safety and the burden of the disease. Of the four considerations it is the least important on its own.

questions.q: When the same test is used in diagnostic and screening situations, which of the following statements is most likely correct?
opts: The sensitivity and specificity will likely be the same in both situations.

This is not reliably true. Sensitivity depends on the spectrum of disease: screening targets early disease, where many tests detect less than in symptomatic patients with advanced disease, so sensitivity is usually lower in screening.
The positive predictive value will be higher in a screening situation.

Positive predictive value is lower in screening, not higher. Screening tests healthy-appearing people with low disease prevalence, so false positives outnumber true positives; positive predictive value rises with prevalence.
Overdiagnosis is equally likely in both situations.

Overdiagnosis (finding disease that would never cause symptoms) is a consequence of screening. It is less likely in diagnostic testing, where symptomatic patients tend to have more advanced disease that is clearly clinically significant.
Disease prevalence will be higher in the diagnostic situation.

Correct. Diagnostic tests are used in symptomatic people, so disease prevalence is higher than among asymptomatic screened people. Higher prevalence raises positive predictive value and lowers negative predictive value.

questions.q: A study found that volunteers for a new screening test had better health outcomes than people who refused testing. Which of the following statements most likely explains the finding?
opts: Volunteers tend to be more interested in their health than those who do not participate in preventive activities.

Correct. This is compliance bias: people who volunteer for screening are more invested in their health and more compliant with advice, so they do better regardless of the test. That is why observational comparisons of volunteers with refusers overstate the benefit of screening.
People who refuse screening are usually healthier than those who accept.

This is backward. There is no reason refusers would be healthier; the pattern reported is that those who decline preventive care tend to have worse outcomes, and health-seeking behavior is what separates the groups.
Volunteers for screening are more likely to need screening than those who refuse.

Greater need for screening would predict worse outcomes in volunteers, not the better outcomes reported here. Screening is aimed at people without symptoms, and the better results reflect compliance bias: people who volunteer are more invested in their health and follow advice more closely.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16; 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 10.11

questions.q: All of the following statements are correct except:
opts: The gold standard for a test used for diagnosis may be different than that for the same test when used for screening.

This statement is true, so it is not the exception. A diagnostic test is usually judged against a single definitive test such as a biopsy, but for a screening test the reference standard almost always involves following people over an interval to see who develops disease.
The incidence method cannot be used to calculate sensitivity for cancer screening tests.

Correct, this is the false statement. The incidence method can be used for the sensitivity of screening tests: people who test negative are followed over an interval, and those who are diagnosed with disease during that interval are the false negatives, so no immediate gold standard is needed for everyone screened.
When a screening program is begun, more people with disease are found on the first round of screening than on later rounds.

This statement is true, so it is not the exception. The first round of screening detects prevalent cases (everyone with existing disease), while later rounds detect mainly incident (new) cases, so the yield is highest at the start.
questions.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 15; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 10.12

questions.q: For a cost-effectiveness analysis of a preventive activity, which kinds of costs should be included?
opts: Medical costs, such as those associated with delivering the preventive intervention

This is true but incomplete. The cost of delivering the preventive activity is one part, but a cost-effectiveness analysis must also include other medical costs (follow-up of positive tests and treatment) and indirect costs.
All medical costs, including diagnostic follow-up of positive tests and treatment for persons diagnosed with disease, with and without the preventive activity
This is true but incomplete. Diagnostic follow-up and treatment costs, with and without prevention, belong in the analysis, but lost income and other indirect costs must also be counted.
Indirect costs, such as loss of income due to time off from work, among patients receiving the prevention and those who develop the disease

This is true but incomplete. Lost income from time off work is a real cost of both prevention and disease, but it is only one category; medical costs of delivering, following up and treating must also be included.
Indirect costs for both patients and care givers
This is true but incomplete. Indirect costs for both patients and caregivers count, but the analysis also needs all direct medical costs, from delivering the prevention to treating disease.
All of the above

Correct. A cost-effectiveness analysis takes a societal perspective and captures all costs: delivery of the preventive activity, diagnostic follow-up and treatment (with and without prevention), and indirect costs for patients and caregivers. Costs without prevention are subtracted from costs with prevention to estimate the cost per health effect.

questions.q: A randomized controlled trial of thrombolytic therapy versus angioplasty for acute myocardial infarction finds no difference in the main outcome, survival to discharge from hospital. The investigators explored whether this was also true for subgroups of patients defined by age, number of vessels affected, ejection fraction, comorbidity, and other patient characteristics. Which of the following is not true about this subgroup analysis?
opts: Examining subgroups increases the chance of a false-positive (misleading statistically significant) result in one of the comparisons.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: each extra subgroup comparison is another chance for a spurious statistically significant result, since at P = 0.05 about 1 in 20 comparisons will look significant by chance alone.
Examining subgroups increases the chance of a false-negative finding in one of these subgroups, relative to the main result.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: subgroups contain far fewer patients than the whole trial, so each has low statistical power and a real effect in one subgroup can easily be missed (a false negative).
Subgroup analyses are bad scientific practice and should not be done.

Correct. This is the statement that is not true. Subgroup analyses carry risks of both false-positive and false-negative conclusions, but with those limits in mind (ideally with the subgroups chosen beforehand and the number of comparisons reported) they give useful information, so they should not be banned.
Reporting results in subgroups helps clinicians tailor information in the study to individual patients.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer: results in subgroups defined by age, number of vessels affected, ejection fraction or comorbidity help clinicians judge whether the average trial result applies to the patient in front of them.

questions.q: A new drug for hyperlipidemia was compared with placebo in a randomized controlled trial of 10,000 patients. After 2 years, serum cholesterol (the primary outcome) was 238 mg/dL in the group receiving the new drug and 240 mg/dL in the group receiving the old drug (P <0.001). Which of the following best describes the meaning of the P value in this study?
opts: Bias is unlikely to account for the observed difference.

The P value addresses only chance (random error). Bias, such as measurement bias or selection bias, is a separate systematic problem, and a very small P value says nothing about whether it is present.
The difference is clinically important.

A P value cannot show clinical importance. A 2 mg/dL difference on a cholesterol of about 240 mg/dL (under 1 percent) is far too small to matter to patients, yet with 10,000 patients it can still be very highly statistically significant.
A difference as big as or bigger than what was observed could have arisen by chance less than one time in 1,000.

Correct. The P value is the probability of seeing a difference this large or larger by chance alone; P < 0.001 means that chance would produce it less than 1 time in 1,000. It says nothing about bias, importance, or generalizability.
The results are generalizable to other patients with hypertension.

The P value does not speak to generalizability, meaning whether results apply to other settings or patients. This trial studied hyperlipidemia, so patients with a different condition such as hypertension are outside what it tested.
The statistical power of this study was inadequate.

Power is about the chance of missing a real difference (a false-negative result). This trial found a highly significant difference, so a missed effect is not the issue, and the P value itself does not measure power.

questions.q: In a well-designed clinical trial of treatment for ovarian cancer, remission rate at 1 year is 30% in patients offered a new drug and 20% in those offered a placebo. The P value is 0.4. Which of the following best describes the interpretation of this result?
opts: Both treatments are effective.

A P value of 0.4 does not show that either treatment works. The 10 percentage point difference (30 percent versus 20 percent) could easily have arisen by chance, so no effectiveness can be claimed for either arm from this result alone.
Neither treatment is effective.

A nonsignificant result does not prove that neither treatment works. The trial may simply have been too small (low power) to detect a real difference, so absence of proof of an effect is not proof of no effect.
The statistical power of this study is 60%.

Power cannot be read from a P value. Power is 1 minus the probability of a type II error and depends on sample size, effect size, event rate and the chosen alpha; the P value of 0.4 gives no information about it.
The best estimate of treatment effect size is 0.4.

The value 0.4 is the P value, a probability, not an effect size. The observed effect is a 10 percentage point higher remission rate (30 percent minus 20 percent), or a ratio of 1.5, and the P value shows only that chance could explain it.
There is insufficient information to decide whether one treatment is better than the other.

Correct. The P value of 0.4 is far above 0.05, so an effect is not established, but it also cannot exclude a real, clinically important effect that a study with too little power missed. The evidence is inconclusive in either direction.

questions.q: In a cohort study, vitamin A intake was found to be a risk factor for hip fracture in women. The relative risk (highest quintile vs. lowest quintile) was 1.48, and the 95% confidence interval was 1.05–2.07. Which of the following best describes the meaning of this confidence interval?
opts: The association is not statistically significant at the P <0.05 level.

The interval 1.05 to 2.07 does not contain 1.0, the value that means no effect for a relative risk, so the result is statistically significant at the 0.05 level (although only just, since the lower limit is barely above 1).
A strong association between vitamin A intake and hip fracture was established.

A relative risk of 1.48 is a modest association, and the lower limit of 1.05 is barely above no effect. Confidence intervals show precision, not proof; this is also a cohort study, so confounding and other bias could still explain it.
The statistical power of this study is 95%.

The 95 percent in a confidence interval is the confidence level, not power. Power is the probability of detecting a real difference (1 minus the type II error probability) and cannot be read from an interval.
There is a 95% chance that a range of relative risks as low as 1.05 and as high as 2.07 includes the true risk.

Correct. A 95 percent confidence interval is a range of values (here relative risks from 1.05 to 2.07) that should contain the true value, with 95 percent confidence. It shows the precision of the estimate.
Bias is an unlikely explanation for this result.

A confidence interval addresses only random error, meaning chance. Bias, such as recall or measurement bias, and confounding are separate problems that a narrow or significant interval does not remove.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best reason for calling P ≤0.05 “statistically significant?”
opts: It definitively rules out a false-positive conclusion.
A P value of 0.05 or less does not rule out a false positive. P = 0.05 means about 1 chance in 20 that a difference this big arose by chance, so a type I error (false positive) can still occur.
It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful rule of thumb.
Correct. The 0.05 cutoff is an arbitrary number that researchers agreed on by convention. It is useful as a rule of thumb, but it has no special mathematical or clinical meaning.
It rules out a type II error.
The P value concerns type I error (false positive). Type II error is a false negative, a separate concept tied to statistical power, and a significance threshold does not rule it out.
It is a way of establishing a clinically important effect size.
Statistical significance says nothing about how large or clinically important an effect is. A tiny difference can have P < 0.05, especially in a large trial, and still be irrelevant to practice.
Larger or smaller P values do not provide useful information.

Other P values are informative: smaller values (0.01, 0.001) mean chance is a less likely explanation, and larger values mean it is more likely. The 0.05 cutoff is just a convention for calling a result significant.

questions.q: Which of the following is the biggest advantage of multivariable modeling?
opts: Models can control for many variables simultaneously.

Correct. Multivariable modeling examines the effect of two or more variables together, so it can take many other variables (confounders or effect modifiers) into account at the same time, which stratified analysis cannot do easily.
Models do not depend on assumptions about the data.
Models depend heavily on assumptions about the data, such as normality and independent errors, and their validity rests on those assumptions holding. That is a limitation, not an advantage.
There is a standardized and reproducible approach to modeling.
There is no single standardized way to build a model. Investigators choose which variables to include and which assumptions to make, so two teams can build different models from the same data.
Models make stratified analyses unnecessary.

Models complement stratified analyses rather than replacing them. Models are also poor at identifying effect modification, which stratifying by the variable makes visible, so stratified analyses remain necessary.
Models can control for confounding in large randomized controlled trials.

In a large randomized trial, randomization has already made confounding very unlikely, so modeling adds little. Modeling matters most in observational studies, where groups are not balanced by chance.

questions.q: A trial randomizes 30,000 patients to two treatment groups of similar size: one offered chemoprevention and the other usual care. How frequently must a side effect of chemoprevention occur for the study to have a good chance of observing at least one such side effect?
opts: Correct. Only about 15,000 people (half of 30,000) receive chemoprevention. The rule of thumb is that observing at least one event needs about 3 divided by the event rate in people; 3 divided by 15,000 is 1 in 5,000, which gives about a 95 percent chance of seeing at least one case.

This uses all 30,000 participants (3 divided by 30,000). Only the 15,000 in the chemoprevention arm are exposed to the drug, so at 1 in 10,000 the chance of seeing even one case is only about 78 percent.

At 1 in 15,000 the expected number of events among 15,000 treated people is only 1, giving about a 63 percent chance of seeing at least one, well short of a good chance. It would need about 45,000 treated people.
At 1 in 20,000 the expected number of events in 15,000 treated people is about 0.75, giving roughly a 53 percent chance of seeing at least one. That is little better than a coin flip.

At 1 in 30,000 the expected number of events among 15,000 treated people is only 0.5, giving about a 39 percent chance of seeing at least one. Rarer side effects generally escape notice in trials of this size.

questions.q: A noninferiority randomized trial compared arthroscopic surgery versus physical therapy for knee injury with meniscal tears. The primary outcome was improvement in knee function, using a scale of 0 to 100, with better function indicated by higher scores. The noninferiority margin was defined as an 8-point difference in improvement, and a one-sided α level was set at 0.025. At 2 years follow-up, the knee surgery group had an improvement in function of 3.6 greater than the physical therapy group, P = 0.001 for noninferiority. Based on the results, which conclusion is true?
opts: There was no clinically important difference between surgery and physical therapy.

Correct. The margin of 8 points is the investigators' judgment of a clinically important difference. The observed difference of 3.6 is below it and the noninferiority test rejected the null hypothesis that physical therapy is worse, so no clinically important difference exists.
There was a statistically significant greater improvement in knee function for the surgery group compared to the physical therapy group.

The reported P value tests noninferiority against the 8-point margin, not whether surgery is better than physical therapy. No test of superiority is reported, and a 3.6-point difference is smaller than the 8 points judged clinically important.
The study could not reject the null hypothesis based on these findings.

The study did reject the null hypothesis. In this design the null hypothesis is that the alternative treatment is worse than the established one by the margin or more; a P value of 0.001, under the one-sided 0.025 level, rejected it.
The study may have erroneously concluded a true difference exists between surgery and physical therapy.

The study did not conclude that a true difference exists; it concluded that physical therapy is not worse than surgery by the 8-point margin. The only error that conclusion could carry is a false claim of noninferiority (type I error), limited by the preset one-sided alpha of 0.025.
A smaller margin would have been more likely to be statistically significant.

A smaller margin makes noninferiority harder to show. With a margin under 3.6, the observed difference would exceed the margin, so the null hypothesis that physical therapy is worse could not be rejected. Small margins also call for larger samples.

questions.q: Which of the following is least related to the statistical power of a study with a dichotomous outcome?
opts: Effect size
Effect size is directly tied to power. A larger true difference between groups is easier to detect, so power rises with effect size and a small expected effect needs more patients.
Type I error

Type I error (alpha) is directly tied to power. Setting a stricter threshold, such as 0.01 instead of 0.05, makes a significant result harder to reach and lowers power unless the sample size is increased.
Rate of outcome events in the control group
The control-group event rate is directly tied to power. With a dichotomous outcome, more events give more information, so a low rate of events in the control group lowers power.
Type II error
Type II error is directly tied to power, because power equals 1 minus the probability of a type II error. A type II error probability of 0.20 gives a power of 0.80.
The statistical test used

Correct. The statistical test used can change the calculated power slightly but is not a main determinant. Power depends mainly on effect size, event rate, the type I error level and the type II error level, which together set sample size.

questions.q: Investigators derive a model to predict postoperative mortality from data on a cohort of patients undergoing surgery for hip fractures. The final model includes variables for heart function (ejection fraction), kidney function (creatinine), and age. Asthma was assessed for inclusion in the model, but did not affect the prediction. The model was found to have excellent discrimination (sensitivity = 0.91, specificity = 0.93, c-statistic = 0.88) and internal calibration. Which of the following is true?
opts: The positive predictive values can be calculated from the provided performance characteristics.

Positive predictive value depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and specificity. Prevalence of postoperative death is not given, so positive predictive values cannot be calculated from those characteristics alone.
The model performance indicates that it would be useful for risk stratification.

Good performance in the derivation cohort does not show the model is useful for risk stratification. It has only been checked internally, so it needs independent validation in other populations before use.
Asthma is a confounder and thus excluded from the final model.

Asthma is not a confounder here. A confounder is linked to both an exposure and the outcome and is adjusted for. In a prediction model, asthma was simply left out because it did not improve the prediction.
Age confounds the other model variables and could be removed from the prediction model.

Age is a variable that improves the prediction of mortality, so it belongs in the model. Removing it would weaken prediction. Confounding describes a distorted exposure-outcome relationship, not variables that jointly predict.
Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study.

Correct. A prediction model keeps the variables that each improve prediction of the outcome, so age, creatinine and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study, and asthma is not.
questions.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 11.10

questions.q: Which of the following best characterizes the application of Bayesian reasoning to a clinical trial?
opts: Prior belief in the comparative effectiveness of treatment is guided by equipoise.

Equipoise is the ethical basis for randomizing: there is no conclusive evidence that either treatment is better, so randomization is acceptable. It is not what Bayesian reasoning is about, which is how new evidence revises belief.
The results of each new study change belief in treatment effect from what it was before the study.

Correct. Bayesian reasoning starts from a prior belief about the treatment effect and updates it with each new study, so belief after the study differs from belief before it. The same idea appears when a test result changes pretest probability into post-test probability.
Bayesian inference is an alternative way of calculating a P value.

Bayesian inference is not another way of calculating a P value. A P value is the probability of a result as large as observed by chance if there is no difference; Bayesian reasoning instead updates prior belief with new data.
Bayesian reasoning is based, like inferential statistics, on the null hypothesis.

Basing conclusions on the null hypothesis of no difference is the approach of frequentist inferential statistics, which uses P values. Bayesian reasoning updates prior beliefs, so it is not built on the null hypothesis.
Bayesian reasoning depends on a well-defined hypothesis before the study is begun.

A well-defined hypothesis before the study describes standard hypothesis testing. Bayesian reasoning is defined by revising a prior belief with new evidence, which is not the same as requiring a hypothesis stated in advance.
questions.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 33; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 11.11

questions.q: In a randomized trial of intensive glucose lowering in type 2 diabetes, death rate was higher in the intensively treated patients: hazard ratio 1.22 (95% confidence interval 1.01–1.46). Which of the following is not true about this study?
opts: The results are consistent with almost no effect.
This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The lower limit of 1.01 is barely above 1.0 (no effect), so the data are compatible with an increase in death rate of only about 1 percent.
The best estimate of treatment effect is a hazard ratio of 1.22.

This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The best estimate of the effect is the point estimate, a hazard ratio of 1.22, which lies inside the interval and means about a 22 percent higher death rate with intensive treatment.
If a P value were calculated, the results would be statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The interval 1.01 to 1.46 excludes 1.0, the value meaning no effect, so a P value would be below 0.05.
A P value would provide as much information as the confidence interval.

Correct. This statement is not true. A P value tells only whether chance is a plausible explanation. The interval also gives the point estimate and the range of effects consistent with the data, so it carries more information.
The results are consistent with 46% higher death rates in the intensively treated patients.
This statement is true, so it is not the answer. The upper confidence limit of 1.46 means the results are consistent with a death rate up to 46 percent higher in the intensively treated group.
