questions.q: One of your patients read that cell phones cause brain cancer, and she wants to know your opinion. You discover that the incidence of malignant brain tumors is increasing in the United States. Results of several observational studies of cell phone use and brain cancer have not agreed with each other. A randomized controlled trial might resolve the question. What is the main reason why a randomized controlled trial (RCT) would be unlikely for this question?
opts: It would cost too much.

A randomized trial of this question would be expensive, and cost is a listed limitation of trials, but it is not the main obstacle; a large study can be funded, whereas assigning people to a possibly harmful exposure cannot be done at any price.
People would not agree to be randomized to cell phone use.

Correct. Randomly assigning people to a potentially harmful exposure such as heavy cell phone use is an ethical problem, and people would not accept long-term restrictions on using their phones. Experimental studies of risk in humans are limited by ethical constraints, so observational designs are used instead.
It would take too long.

Time is a practical limitation of trials, and a cancer with a long latency would need long follow-up, but that is a difficulty and not the main barrier; the decisive barrier is that people cannot ethically or realistically be randomized to a possibly harmful exposure.
Even if done well, a randomized trial could not answer the question.

This is false. A well-done randomized trial is the strongest design for showing cause and effect because random assignment balances other factors between groups; the reason no such trial is likely here is ethics and willingness to participate, not an inability of the design to answer the question.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 8; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.1

questions.q: Which of the following would be least consistent with the belief that cell phone use is a cause of brain cancer?
opts: A dose–response relationship
A dose-response relationship (larger exposure, higher rate of disease) would be consistent with cell phones causing brain cancer, because it is one of the criteria that raise belief in causation.
A large effect size (such as relative risk)

A large effect size, such as a large relative risk, would be consistent with cause, because strength of the association is one of the criteria for causality and large associations are harder to explain by confounding alone.
Separate analyses of patients with right- and left-sided tumors in relation to the side they usually listened to their cell phone

Analyzing tumors by the side of the head where the phone is usually held would test the hypothesis directly; tumors clustering on the exposed side would support causation, and this kind of check bears on the causal criteria, making a cause more or less believable.
A biologic explanation for why cell phones might cause cancer
A biologic explanation for how phones might cause cancer would support the hypothesis, because biologic plausibility is one of the criteria for causality (the relationship makes sense biologically).
Cell phone use is associated with many different kinds of cancers

Correct. An exposure associated with many different cancers lacks specificity (one cause leading to one effect), which counts for less than the other criteria listed; many well-established causes, such as cigarette smoking, produce several diseases, so lack of specificity only weakly argues against a cause.
questions.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.2

questions.q: Which of the following is the most accurate description of a causal relationship?
opts: Tuberculosis has a single cause, the tubercle bacillus.

Not correct. The tubercle bacillus is a necessary cause (without it, tuberculosis cannot occur), but it is not sufficient: many exposed people never develop the disease, so host and environmental factors also matter. A necessary cause that is present may or may not lead to disease.
Most genetic diseases are caused only by an abnormal gene.

Not correct. Nearly all diseases are caused by the joint effect of genes and environment, so an abnormal gene is usually only one contributor; even in single-gene disorders, whether and how severely disease appears often depends on other genes and environmental exposures, which is the web-of-causation view.
Coronary heart disease has multiple interacting causes.

Correct. Coronary heart disease is caused by several risk factors acting together, a web of causation with multiple causes. A risk factor raises the probability of disease in a group and is neither necessary nor sufficient by itself.
Effective treatment has been the main cause of decline in tuberculosis rates.

Not correct. Tuberculosis rates fell steeply long before effective drug treatment became available in the 1950s, so treatment cannot be the main cause of the decline; other factors, such as living conditions, were changing the rate.
questions.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 24; 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.3

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of the Bradford Hill criteria for causation?
opts: Dose–response
Dose-response is one of the criteria for causality: a larger exposure leading to a higher rate of disease supports a cause-and-effect relationship, so it does belong on the list.
Statistical significance

Correct. Statistical significance is not a causal criterion. It only shows that an association is unlikely to be due to chance, whereas the causal criteria (temporality, strength, dose-response, reversibility, consistency, biologic plausibility, specificity, analogy) judge whether an association is cause and effect.
Reversibility
Reversibility is one of the criteria for causality: decreased exposure leading to less disease supports a cause-and-effect relationship, so it does belong on the list.
Biologic plausibility
Biologic plausibility is one of the criteria for causality: the relationship should make sense biologically, so it does belong on the list.
Analogy
Analogy is one of the criteria for causality: a similar cause and effect pattern for a similar exposure and disease supports cause, so it does belong on the list.
questions.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.4

questions.q: A study of the colorectal cancer screening comparing fecal occult blood testing to no screening finds that screening costs $20,000 per year of life saved. This study is an example of which of the following?
opts: Cost–benefit analysis

Cost-benefit analysis expresses both the costs and the benefits in money. This study reports its result per year of life saved, a clinical effect and not a dollar value, so it is not cost-benefit analysis.
Decision analysis

Decision analysis is a method of comparing the possible outcomes of alternative choices; it is not the name for a study reporting a cost per unit of clinical benefit, which is what $20,000 per year of life saved describes.
Cost-effectiveness analysis

Correct. Cost-effectiveness analysis describes financial costs per clinical effect, here dollars per year of life saved, for alternative tests or treatments (here fecal occult blood testing compared with no screening).
A clinical decision rule

A clinical decision rule is a tool that helps clinicians reach a decision from patient findings; it does not measure the cost of an intervention per year of life saved, so it does not describe this study.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.5

questions.q: Which of the following is true about aggregate risk studies?
opts: Aggregate risk studies are not susceptible to confounding.

This is false. Studies that compare groups are still vulnerable to confounding, because other characteristics of the groups can differ along with the exposure, and averaging across a group hides which individuals carry those other factors.
Multiple time-series studies cannot provide strong evidence of cause and effect.

This is too absolute. Time-series studies, which follow a rate before and after a change, can support cause when other explanations, such as other changes in local conditions at the same time, have been ruled out; they are not automatically weak.
Studies relating average exposure to average risk can provide a strong test of a causal hypothesis.

This is false. When exposure and disease are measured as group averages, the people who got the disease may not be the ones who were exposed, so such studies are better for generating hypotheses than for a strong test of cause.
An ecological fallacy might affect their validity.

Correct. Aggregate (ecologic) studies measure exposure and disease in groups, not individuals, so the ecologic fallacy is possible: applying group-level data to an individual, when the affected people may not have been the exposed ones.
questions.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.6

questions.q: Which of the following would weaken belief that the “MRSA package” (see graph) caused the observed decline in MRSA infections in VA acute care hospitals?
opts: Better antibiotics became available around the time of the program.

Correct. Better antibiotics arriving at about the same time is another change that could explain the decline, and the alternative explanations for an association must be excluded before the program can be credited. In a time-series study, changes in local conditions at about the same time weaken the causal conclusion.
Hand washing, a part of the MRSA package, increased after the program was introduced.

More hand washing after the program began would strengthen the belief in cause, because it shows the program's components were carried out and fits a biologically plausible route by which the package lowers infections.
The rate of MRSA infections was stable for the years before the program was introduced.

A stable rate before the program would strengthen the belief in cause, because the decline is then a new change and not the continuation of a downward trend that was already under way (in the graph the rate fluctuated without falling before the program).
Decline in rates began just after the program was introduced.

A decline that began just after the program started fits the temporal relationship, the cause preceding the effect, which is a criterion for causality, so it would strengthen and not weaken belief in cause.

questions.alt: Health-care-associated MRSA infections per 1,000 patient-days from October 2005 to June 2010, falling after the program was introduced across the VA hospitals.

questions.q: Randomized controlled trials are the strongest research designs for establishing cause and effect. Which of the following is the main limitation of trials for this purpose?
opts: Clinical trials may not be ethical or feasible for some questions.

Correct. Randomized trials are the strongest design for cause and effect when done well, but they are often impossible because studies of harm are unethical and people may be unwilling to take part. Experimental studies of risk in humans are limited by ethical constraints.
Randomized trials cannot control for unmeasured confounders.

This is not accurate. Random assignment is what lets a trial balance unmeasured as well as measured factors between groups, which is why it is the strongest design; only small trials may show residual confounding by chance, and that is not the main limitation.
Type of study design is only a crude measure of the scientific strength.

Design type is indeed only a rough guide to strength, but that caveat applies to the ranking of all designs and is not a limitation specific to trials. The question asks about the main limitation of trials for establishing cause, which is that they are frequently unethical or infeasible.
Results of poorly designed and conducted trials are no better than for observational studies.

Poorly designed or conducted trials can indeed be weak, but that reflects execution and not the design. A well-designed and well-conducted trial remains the strongest evidence; the main limitation is that trials cannot be done for many suspected causes.
questions.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 8; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 13; 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.8

questions.q: Which of the following provides the strongest evidence for a cause-and- effect relationship?
opts: Observational studies that have controlled for bias and minimized the role of chance.

Observational studies that control bias and chance are needed, but they show an association; they still leave open whether it is cause and effect, which requires considering the causal criteria together.
A biologic mechanism can explain the relationship.
A biologic mechanism, biologic plausibility, is one criterion for causality and supports a cause, but by itself it is weaker than the whole pattern of evidence.
The purported cause clearly precedes the effect.
Temporality, the cause preceding the effect, is necessary for causation, but it is only one criterion; a cause coming first does not by itself show the exposure produced the outcome.
There is a dose–response relationship.
A dose-response relationship raises belief in cause, but it is a single criterion; it is stronger when combined with the others than when it stands alone.
The evidence as a whole is consistent with the Bradford Hill criteria.
Correct. The more criteria for causality that are met, the stronger the case for cause and effect; the pattern of evidence across all the criteria is more powerful than evidence for any one of them.
questions.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 12.9

questions.q: You discover that case-control studies have been done to determine whether cell phone use is associated with the development of brain cancer. In one study, patients with brain cancer and matched controls without brain cancer were asked about cell phone use. The estimated relative risk for at least 100 hours of use compared to no use was 1.0 for all types of brain cancers combined (95% confidence interval 0.6–1.5). This finding is consistent with all of the following except:
opts: Use of cell phones increases the incidence of brain cancers by 50%.
This result is consistent with a 50% increase, because the upper confidence limit of 1.5 corresponds to a 50% higher risk; the interval includes values that would mean harm.
Use of cell phones protects against brain cancers.
This result is consistent with protection, because the lower confidence limit of 0.6 corresponds to a 40% lower risk; the interval includes values that would mean benefit.
Specific types of cancers might be associated with cell phone use.
This result is consistent with specific types being associated, because the estimate pools all brain cancers together, and a risk in one subtype could be hidden by the combined analysis.
The study has adequate statistical power to answer the research question.

Correct (this is the statement that does not fit). An interval of 0.6 to 1.5 is wide, running from clear benefit to clear harm, which shows imprecision and too little statistical power; a study with adequate power would give a narrower interval, so the null result cannot be trusted as showing no association.

questions.q: A systematic review of observational studies of antioxidant vitamins to prevent cardiovascular disease combined the results of 12 studies to obtain a summary effect size and confidence interval. Which of the following would be the strongest rationale for combining study results?
opts: You wish to obtain a more generalizable conclusion.

Pooling can make the conclusion somewhat more generalizable because results come from more than one time and place, but that is not the main reason to combine studies. The main gain is statistical: a larger combined sample gives a more precise estimate.
A statistical test shows that the studies are heterogeneous.

A statistical test showing heterogeneity is a reason for caution, not a rationale for pooling. Studies to be combined must be similar, and a significant heterogeneity test means the effect sizes differ more than chance allows, so pooling is questionable or needs a random effects approach.
Most of the component studies are statistically significant.

Whether the component studies are individually statistically significant is not a reason to combine them. Pooling is done to improve precision and power, which matters most when single studies are too small to be conclusive on their own.
The component studies have different, and to some extent complementary, biases.

Pooling does not cancel biases. A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it includes, and biases shared by observational studies, such as confounding, carry into the summary estimate, so complementary biases are not a justification for combining.
You can obtain a more precise estimate of effect size.

Correct. Meta-analysis weights and pools the numerical results of similar studies, so the larger combined sample gives a stronger, more precise estimate of effect size (a narrower confidence interval) than any single study can.

questions.q: You are asked to critique a review of the literature on whether alcohol is a risk factor for breast cancer. The reviewer has searched MEDLINE and found several observational studies of this question but has not searched elsewhere. All of the following are limitations of this search strategy except:
opts: Studies with negative results tend to not be published.

This is a real limitation. Research without statistically significant results is less likely to be published, so a search of published literature misses those studies and tilts the evidence toward positive findings; a database search cannot correct it.
MEDLINE searches typically miss some articles, even those included in the database.
This is a real limitation. Even for articles that are in MEDLINE, a search will not retrieve every relevant one, so a reviewer relying on a single search strategy can overlook eligible studies.
MEDLINE does not include all of the world's journals.

This is a real limitation. MEDLINE covers a large share of the medical literature but not all of the world's journals, so relevant studies published elsewhere are missed unless other databases and sources are also searched.
MEDLINE can be simultaneously searched for both content area and methods.

Correct, this is the exception. Being able to search MEDLINE for both the content area and study methods at once is a strength that helps narrow a search, not a limitation. The limitations are missed articles, incomplete journal coverage, and publication bias.

questions.q: A systematic review of antiplatelet drugs for cardiovascular disease prevention combined individual patients, not trials. Which of the following is an advantage of this approach?
opts: It allows for ecological comparisons.

Ecological comparisons compare group-level characteristics, which risks applying aggregate data to individuals (the ecologic fallacy). Pooling individual patients does the opposite and lets analysis be done at the level of the person, which avoids that problem.
It is more efficient for the investigator.

Efficiency is not the benefit of pooling patients instead of trials. The gain is analytic, in that combined patient-level data can be analyzed in ways summary results cannot, most notably by subgroup.
Subgroup analyses are possible.

Correct. Individual trials are usually too small to examine subgroups, but pooling patients from several trials gives enough people in each subgroup to compare effects, and meta-analysis is noted for detecting differences in subgroups. This works only when patients, not trials, are pooled.
It is not necessary to choose between fixed and random effects models when combining data.

The choice between the fixed effect model and the random effects model depends on whether the studies show heterogeneity (fixed effect when there is none, random effects when it is present), and pooling patients does not remove the need to consider it.
Publication bias is less likely.

Publication bias arises because studies without significant results are less likely to be published. Pooling individual patients from the trials that are available does not bring in unpublished trials, so this approach does not by itself make publication bias less likely.

questions.q: Which of the following is not generally used to define a specific clinical question studied by randomized controlled trials?
opts: Covariates that were taken into account

Correct. A specific clinical question is defined by PICO: patients, intervention, comparison, and outcomes. Covariates are not part of the question; they bear on how well the question can be answered, such as by confounding or effect modification.
Interventions (e.g., exposure or experimental treatment)

The intervention or exposure is the I in PICO (patients, intervention, comparison, outcomes): the main intervention, prognostic factor, or exposure being considered. It is used to define the clinical question.
Comparison group (e.g., patients taking placebo in a randomized trial)
The comparison group is the C in PICO (patients, intervention, comparison, outcomes): the main alternative to the intervention, such as placebo. It is used to define the clinical question.
Outcomes
The outcome is the O in PICO (patients, intervention, comparison, outcomes): what the investigators hope to measure, improve, or affect. It is used to define the clinical question.
Patients in the trials
The patients or population are the P in PICO (patients, intervention, comparison, outcomes): the group of patients similar to the one in question. They are used to define the clinical question.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes ways of measuring study quality?
opts: The validity of summary measures of study quality is well established.

Combining individual quality items into one summary score is less well established than describing them, in part because it is not meaningful to give every element the same weight. Scoring systems exist but their validity is not settled.
A description of study quality is a useful part of systematic reviews.

Correct. A good systematic review describes each included study's characteristics and risk of bias, so readers can judge how strong the conclusions are. Assessing the quality of the included studies is a standard step in evaluating a review.
In a summary measure of quality, strengths of the study can make up for weaknesses.

A summary score adds strengths and weaknesses together, but a strength in one area does not repair a fatal weakness in another. A flaw such as failure to randomize can still distort the result no matter how large the sample is.
Individual measures of quality such as randomization and blinding are not associated with study results.

Quality elements such as randomization and blinding are assessed precisely because weaknesses can bias results. For example, blinding of participants protects against performance bias, so these features are tied to how trustworthy the results are.

questions.q: Which of the following kinds of studies is least likely to be published?
opts: Small positive studies

Small studies with positive results are more likely to be published than small studies with no effect, because research with statistically significant results is favored for publication. They are not the least likely to be published.
Large negative studies
Large studies tend to be published whatever they find, because of their size and importance, so a large negative study is not among the least likely to be published.
Large positive studies
Large positive studies are very likely to be published, since both size and a significant result favor publication.
Small negative studies

Correct. Research without statistically significant results is less likely to be published, and small studies do not carry enough weight to overcome this, whereas large studies are usually published regardless of their findings. This is the core of publication bias.
questions.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 46; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 13.6

questions.q: Which of the following is a comparative advantage of traditional (“narrative”) reviews over systematic reviews?
opts: Readers can confirm that evidence cited is selected without bias.

This describes a systematic review, not a narrative review. Systematic reviews use explicit inclusion criteria and list excluded studies so readers can check selection. In narrative reviews cited articles may have been selected to prove a point of view.
Narrative reviews can review a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition.

Correct. Narrative reviews can address broad topics and a range of issues, such as the whole set of questions involved in caring for a condition. The cost is an unstructured approach with no transparent description of how the evidence was chosen.
They rely on the experience and judgment of an expert in the field.

Authors' clinical experience is a real feature of narrative reviews, but it cuts both ways, because information may then be shaped by the authors' values and personal experience. The advantage that systematic reviews cannot match is covering a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition.
They provide a quantitative summary of effects.

A quantitative summary of effects is a feature of meta-analysis, which weights and pools numerical results from similar studies. Narrative reviews are unstructured and typically do not calculate a summary effect.
The scientific strength of the studies cited is explicitly evaluated.

Explicit evaluation of the scientific strength of studies is a feature of systematic reviews, which describe each study's risk of bias. Narrative reviews may not include a critique of the original research.

questions.q: Which of the following is not always part of a typical forest plot?
opts: The number of studies that meet inclusion criteria for quality

The studies included in the review each appear on the plot, one row per study, so the number of included studies is visible; this is part of how a forest plot summarizes the raw evidence. It is not the element that is sometimes left out.
A summary or pooled effect size with confidence interval

Correct. A pooled (summary) effect with its confidence interval, shown as a diamond, is included only if pooling is justified. If the studies are too different, the plot shows the individual studies without combining them.
Point estimates of effect size for each study
The point estimate of effect size for each study is always shown, typically as a square or dot, and is a basic element of a forest plot.
Confidence intervals for each study
Each study's confidence interval is always shown as a horizontal line through its point estimate, so it is a standard element of every forest plot.
The size or weight contributed by each study
The size or weight each study contributes is always conveyed, usually by the size of the marker, because studies are weighted in proportion to their size.
questions.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 13.8

questions.q: Which of the following cannot be used for identifying severity of illness as a reason for heterogeneity in a systematic review with meta-analysis?
opts: Controlling for severity of illness in a study-level meta-analysis

Correct. In a study-level meta-analysis only summary data from each study are available, so you cannot control for a covariate such as severity of illness as could be done in a single study or in a patient-level analysis. You can only compare studies with different average severities.
A mathematical model relating average severity of illness to outcome across the component studies
Relating average severity of illness to the outcome across the studies is metaregression, a recognized way to explore reasons for differences between studies (heterogeneity) at the study level.
A comparison of summary effect sizes in studies stratified by mean severity of illness
Comparing summary effects in studies grouped by mean severity is a subgroup analysis, which is one of the recognized ways to identify the reasons for differences between studies.
Subgroup analyses of patient-level data
Subgroup analyses of patient-level data are possible because the individual patients can be separated by severity, which is one advantage of pooling patients rather than trials.
questions.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 13.9

questions.q: Which of the following is the best justification for combining the results of five studies into a single summary effect?
opts: A statistical test does not detect heterogeneity.

A nonsignificant heterogeneity test is not reassurance with only five studies, because the test has low power to detect differences among so few studies. Pooling is justified by whether the studies are actually similar.
All studies are of high quality.
Studies can all be of high quality yet differ in the patients enrolled, the interventions given, or the outcomes measured. Quality does not make dissimilar studies combinable.
The patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar.

Correct. Studies must be similar in order to be pooled, and this is judged by informed review of the patients, interventions, and outcomes rather than by a statistic alone. Combining dissimilar studies can be misleading.
Publication bias has been ruled out by a funnel plot.

A funnel plot assesses publication and reporting bias, not clinical similarity. Even a reassuring funnel plot would not show that the patients, interventions, and outcomes are similar enough to combine.
The random effects model will be used to calculate the summary effect size.

A random effects model is a way to calculate the summary once pooling is decided, and it allows for variation among studies. It does not make dissimilar studies suitable for combining, because pooling studies that are not similar can still mislead.
questions.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 24; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 13.10

questions.q: Which of the following is most correct for network meta-analyses?
opts: Multiple interventions are directly compared to each other and ranked.

Network meta-analyses can rank several interventions, but the comparisons are not all direct. Many are inferred indirectly through a shared comparator, so the network combines direct and indirect evidence rather than comparing every intervention head to head.
They require individual-level patient data for the analysis.
They do not require individual-level data. Network meta-analyses can use study-level or patient-level data, so this requirement is false.
They require randomized controlled trials for analysis.
They do not require randomized controlled trials. Network meta-analyses can use observational or randomized data, so this requirement is false.
They do not require similar interventions for analysis.

Correct. The interventions in a network meta-analysis can be diverse. What matters is that the studies address similar patients and similar outcomes, which allows both direct and indirect comparisons among the interventions or tests.
They show the additional effects of new studies on the summary estimate.
Showing the added effect of each new study on the summary estimate describes a cumulative meta-analysis, which adds studies one at a time. A network meta-analysis compares multiple interventions.
questions.cite: Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 13.11

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of the random effects model over the fixed effect model?
opts: It can be used for studies with time-to-event analyses.

Both models can be applied to time-to-event outcomes, so this is not a special advantage of the random effects model. The choice between the two depends on the heterogeneity among studies, not on the type of outcome.
It describes the summary effect size for a single, narrowly defined question.

This describes the fixed effect model, which assumes a fixed magnitude of effect for one narrowly defined question, with variation attributed to chance. The random effects model allows for variation not due to chance.
It is better suited for meta-analyses of diagnostic test performance.

Suitability for diagnostic test performance is not what distinguishes the two models; the deciding factor is whether heterogeneity is present. The random effects model is used when it is, whatever the kind of study.
Confidence intervals tend to be narrower.

Random effects models give wider, not narrower, confidence intervals, because they account for variation between studies. The narrower intervals belong to the fixed effect model, which is why they can be falsely reassuring when studies differ.
It gives more realistic results when there is heterogeneity among studies.

Correct. The random effects model allows for variation among studies that is not due to chance, and so is used when heterogeneity is present. It gives wider confidence intervals that are more likely to be accurate than the narrower ones a fixed effect model would give.
questions.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 24; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 13.12

questions.q: You are finishing residency and will begin practice. You want to establish a plan for keeping up with new developments in your field even though there are few professional colleagues in your community. All of the following might be useful, but which will be most useful to you?
opts: Subscribe to a few good journals.

Journals are one way to keep current, but more than 30,000 medical journals and over 2 million studies exist, so a few subscriptions cannot cover all the strong, relevant new research; a service that screens and summarizes the literature does that work for you.
Subscribe to a service that reviews the literature in your field.

Correct. It is virtually impossible to keep up with all scientifically strong, clinically relevant new research alone, so a service that reviews the literature in your field does the screening and summarizing for you, which matters most when few colleagues are nearby.
Buy new editions of printed textbooks.

Printed textbooks are fixed at the time of printing, so they are prone to outdated evidence, a recognized challenge of evidence-based practice; a new edition does not track developments as they appear.
Search MEDLINE at regular intervals.

MEDLINE holds more than 19 million citations, so searching it at intervals is inefficient for surveillance; it suits looking up a specific question or a rare event, not routinely keeping up with a whole field.
Keep up contacts with colleagues in your training program by e-mail and telephone.

Colleagues are a legitimate way to keep current, but the stem says few are nearby, and occasional calls or e-mail do not systematically capture new strong research the way a dedicated literature-review service does.
questions.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 6; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 14.1

questions.q: You can rely on the best general medical journals in your field to:
opts: Provide answers to clinical questions.

Journals mostly report single original studies and are not efficient for answering an immediate question; answers come better from systematic reviews, practice guidelines, or an evidence-based synopsis from a credible resource.
Assure that you have kept up with the medical literature.
With more than 30,000 medical journals and over 2 million studies published, reading even the best general journals leaves large gaps, so they cannot assure you have kept up with the literature.
Guarantee that the information they contain is beyond reproach.

Journals cannot guarantee that; a Lancet study linking the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine to autism was retracted after undisclosed financial conflicts and unapproved procedures came to light, and peer review helps but does not make articles flawless.
Expose you to the many dimensions of your profession.

Correct. The best general journals are a rich source of information on the many dimensions of being a physician, including history, politics, science, ideas, and experiences, even though they are not good for immediate answers or surveillance.
questions.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 14.2

questions.q: Many children in your practice have attacks of otitis media. You want to base your management on the best available evidence. Which of the following is the least credible source of information on this question?
opts: A clinical practice guideline by a major medical society

A good guideline gives its recommendations together with the supporting evidence and rationale, and trustworthy guidelines rest on systematic reviews, so a major society guideline is a credible source, not the least credible.
A systematic review published in a major journal

Good systematic reviews and meta-analyses provide the highest level of evidence because they combine many studies to answer a specific, focused question, so a systematic review is among the most credible sources.
The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews

The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews belongs to the Cochrane Library, a listed evidence-based medicine resource named for Archie Cochrane, who advocated systematic reviews to verify treatment effectiveness, so it is a highly credible source, not the weakest.
The most recent research article on this question

Correct. A single recent article, seen out of context with the other studies on the same question, sits lower in the hierarchy than syntheses and is of marginal value unless it is much stronger than all the studies before it.
questions.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 35; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 4; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 14.3

questions.q: A search of MEDLINE is especially useful for which of the following?
opts: Finding all of the best articles bearing on a clinical question

A MEDLINE search returns citations without grading their quality, and it is only one part of an effort to find every published article on a question, so a search alone does not find all of the best articles.
An efficient strategy for finding the good articles

Searching a database of more than 19 million citations is inefficient for most questions at the point of care; a systematic review or an evidence-based synopsis from a credible resource is the faster route to good articles.
Looking for reports of rare events

Correct. A targeted search is indispensable for learning whether a rare event has been reported, because a specific query can locate even a single case report among millions of citations; it is too inefficient for most questions at the point of care.
Keeping up with the medical literature

The volume of literature (over 19 million MEDLINE citations) is far too large to keep up with by searching; keeping current is better done through a review service, professional organizations, and similar sources.
Being familiar with the medical profession as a whole

Becoming familiar with the profession as a whole comes from reading broadly, such as general medical journals that cover its history, ideas, and experiences; a database search returns narrow citations on a topic.
questions.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 16; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 14.4

questions.q: Which of the following is accomplished by peer review of research manuscripts before they are published?
opts: Exclude articles by authors with a conflict of interest.

Peer review does not exclude authors with conflicts of interest; conflicts are supposed to be disclosed so readers can judge whether bias is present, and the peer review process only helps limit their effects.
Make the published article accurate and trustworthy.

Correct, as the best available answer. Peer review and editing make articles more readable, accurate, and complete, and it is an accepted marker of quality, but articles remain imperfect after publication.
Relieve readers of the need to be skeptical about the study.

Peer review does not relieve readers of skepticism; the retracted Lancet study on the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine was published, and readers must still judge the validity of the research and the strength of its methods.
Decide for the editors about whether they should publish the manuscript.
Peer reviewers only recommend that a manuscript be rejected, revised, or accepted; the editors review those recommendations and make the publication decision.
questions.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 14.5

questions.q: An author of an article showing that screening colonoscopy is more effective in preventing colorectal cancer than other forms of screening would have conflicts of interest if he or she had any of the following except:
opts: Clinical income from performing colonoscopies
Income from performing colonoscopies is a financial conflict of interest, because the author benefits financially if colonoscopy is judged the best screening test.
Investment in a company that makes colonoscopies
Owning stock in a company that makes colonoscopies is a financial conflict of interest, because the author would gain financially from a favorable conclusion about colonoscopy.
Investment in medical products in general

Correct. Conflict of interest relates to a specific activity, and investing in medical products in general is not tied to colonoscopy in particular, so it creates no specific conflict for this conclusion.
Publications of articles that have consistently advocated colonoscopy as the best screening test
A record of publications consistently advocating colonoscopy is a personal, intellectual, and career conflict, because the author has a professional stake in the same conclusion being shown again.
Rivalry with other scholars who advocate another screening test
Rivalry with scholars who favor another screening test is a personal and intellectual conflict, because a wish to defeat competing views can bias how the study is designed and reported.
questions.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 32; 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 14.6

questions.q: Which of the following is the least useful way of looking up answers to clinical questions at the point of care?
opts: Subscribing to several journals and keeping them available where you see patients

Correct. Journals have great value for other reasons, but a stack of them at the bedside is not a fast way to look up an answer, because they mostly report single studies rather than an organized, evidence-graded answer.
Guidelines on http://www.guidelines.gov

Practice guidelines, including the government-sponsored collections that are listed among quality sources, give recommendations with supporting evidence and are a valuable point-of-care source, not the least useful.
The Cochrane Library on the Internet
The Cochrane Library is a listed evidence-based medicine database of systematic reviews, so it is a valuable way to look up answers at the point of care, if a computer is available.
A continually updated electronic textbook
A continually updated electronic textbook, of which UpToDate is a listed example, keeps recommendations current and is quick to search, so it is a valuable point-of-care source.

questions.q: Which of the following should be least reassuring to a patient about the quality of a web site providing information about HIV?
opts: The site is sponsored by a governmental agency and names its advisory board members.

Government sponsorship together with a named advisory board is reassuring, because government databases are listed as quality sources and openly identified reviewers make the site transparent and accountable.
The site provides facts, not opinions.
A site that provides facts instead of opinions is reassuring, because bias and the level of detail in the content are core parts of judging a source, and facts can be checked against a source.
The primary source of information is stated.
Stating the primary source of the information is reassuring, because a reader can verify the facts and judge their validity rather than trusting an unsupported claim.
The date of the last revision is posted and recent.
A posted and recent revision date is reassuring, because a source must still be current, and outdated evidence is a recognized challenge in evidence-based practice.
The author is a well-known expert in the field.

Correct. Fame alone is the least reassuring, because a well-known expert may still be biased; the retracted Lancet vaccine study came from an author with undisclosed conflicts. Look for the sponsoring organization, facts, and stated sources.
questions.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18; 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19; Clinical Epidemiology Study Questions, Question 14.8

questions.q: Which of the following is not part of grading clinical recommendations using the GRADE system?
opts: Deciding whether to use a diagnostic test

Correct. The grading table rates recommendations for treatment by the quality of the evidence and the strength of the recommendation; it is a way to grade evidence, and deciding whether to order a particular diagnostic test remains a clinical judgment rather than a component of the grading.
Takes into account the balance of benefits and harms
Weighing benefits against harms is part of grading; the clarity of risk and benefit determines whether a recommendation is strong or weak, and the process involves weighing pros and cons.
Rates the quality of scientific evidence separately

Rating the quality of the evidence separately is part of grading; quality is the letter grade A to C, reflecting confidence in the estimate of effect, from high (well-performed randomized trials) to low (observational studies).
Suggests how commonly and how forcefully a treatment should be recommended

Suggesting how commonly and how forcefully to recommend a treatment is part of grading; a strong recommendation applies to most patients, whereas a weak one means the best action may differ by patient values.
Rates the strength of the evidence and of recommendations separately

Rating the strength of the recommendation separately from the quality of the evidence is part of grading; strength is the number 1 or 2, so a strong recommendation can rest on low-quality evidence and a weak one on high-quality evidence.

questions.q: A comprehensive approach to managing knowledge in your field would include which of the following?
opts: Subscribing to some journals and browsing them
Subscribing to and browsing journals is one basic element of a comprehensive plan, but it is only part of it; the plan also needs point-of-care lookup, a review publication, and sites for patients.
Establishing a plan for looking up information at the point of care
A plan for looking up information at the point of care is one basic element, but not the whole plan; keeping current and guiding patients to reliable sources are also needed.
Finding a publication that helps you keep up with new developments in your field
A publication that helps you keep up with new developments is one basic element of a comprehensive plan, but not the whole plan; browsing, point-of-care lookup, and patient resources belong as well.
Identifying web sites you can recommend to your patients
Identifying web sites you can recommend to patients is one basic element, since sources must be judged for author, bias, content, and date; on its own it does not manage your own knowledge.
